packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials I
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Full on, all the way: "estoy a full con el laburo". Anglicism, very common and informal.

example.es: Esta semana estoy a full con los exámenes.
example.en: This week I'm very busy with exams.

words.note: Internet and teen slang added at the end of a sentence to mark it as a joke or irony.

example.es: Mañana renuncio y me voy a vivir a Bali, ahre.
example.en: Tomorrow I quit and move to Bali, just kidding.

words.note: Very common: "voy al toque", I'm coming right now. Informal.

example.es: Esperame, que bajo al toque.
example.en: Wait for me, I'll be right down.

words.note: Placed before a noun for emphasis: "alto quilombo", "alta fiesta". Young, very informal.

example.es: Anoche fue alta fiesta en lo de Juli.
example.en: Last night was a huge party at Juli's.

words.note: Super common way to say great or fine: "¡Bárbaro!". Can also mean extreme.

example.es: ¡Bárbaro! Nos vemos a las ocho en la esquina.
example.en: Great! See you at eight on the corner.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials II
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: A mess, trouble or fight. "Se armó bardo": things got ugly. "¡Qué bardo!": what a hassle.

example.es: Se armó un bardo bárbaro en la salida del boliche.
example.en: A huge mess broke out outside the club.

words.note: Cheap, crappy, low quality. Works for objects, ideas or people.

example.es: Me compré unos auriculares berretas y ya se rompieron.
example.en: I bought some cheap headphones and they already broke.

words.note: Nonsense or a trivial thing. "No digas boludeces": don't talk nonsense. Informal.

example.es: Nos peleamos por una boludez.
example.en: We fought over a silly thing.

words.note: How Argentines say good morning, more than "buenos días".

example.es: Buen día, ¿me da medio kilo de pan?
example.en: Good morning, can I have half a kilo of bread?

words.note: Describes a friendly, easygoing person or vibe: "es re buena onda". Opposite: "mala onda".

example.es: El profe nuevo es re buena onda.
example.en: The new teacher is really nice.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials III
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Filler to wrap up or change topic when there is nothing more to say. Very typical porteño rhythm.

example.es: Bueno, nada, eso te quería contar. Hablamos después.
example.en: Well, anyway, that's what I wanted to tell you. Talk later.

words.note: Informal for oppressive heat. Summer in Buenos Aires is famous for it.

example.es: ¡Qué calorón! Vamos a buscar un aire acondicionado.
example.en: It's so hot! Let's find some air conditioning.

words.note: Argentines usually call their language "castellano" rather than "español".

example.es: Mi amiga inglesa habla castellano mejor que yo.
example.en: My English friend speaks Spanish better than I do.

words.note: Before a noun for emphasis: "cero ganas", "cero onda". Informal, very common.

example.es: Hoy tengo cero ganas de cocinar, pidamos algo.
example.en: I have zero desire to cook today, let's order something.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials IV
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Flattery or made-up talk. "Es puro chamuyo" means it's all BS.

example.es: Eso de que te llamó es puro chamuyo.
example.en: That story about him calling you is all lies.

words.note: The most Argentine word of all, used to get attention or like "man".

example.es: Che, ¿me pasás la sal?
example.en: Hey, can you pass me the salt?

words.note: Gossip, especially about famous people. TV has whole "programas de chimentos".

example.es: Mi vieja mira todos los programas de chimentos.
example.en: My mom watches every celebrity gossip show.

words.note: The usual greeting with voseo. Reply: "bien, ¿y vos?".

example.es: Hola, Juli, ¿cómo andás? Tanto tiempo.
example.en: Hi Juli, how's it going? Long time no see.

words.note: Nice, fun or kind. Used for people, places and plans.

example.es: Tu amiga es re copada, invitala de nuevo.
example.en: Your friend is really cool, invite her again.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials V
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Used for anything whose name you forget. Also a mildly rude "that guy".

example.es: Pasame el coso ese que está arriba de la mesa.
example.en: Pass me that thing on the table.

words.note: "¡Cualquiera!" or "qué cualquiera": that's ridiculous, makes no sense. Also "hacer cualquiera": act crazy.

example.es: ¿Te cobraron diez lucas por un café? ¡Cualquiera!
example.en: They charged you ten thousand pesos for a coffee? That's ridiculous!

words.note: Means OK, sure, or come on! Probably the word you'll hear most.

example.es: ¿Nos vemos a las ocho? Dale, perfecto.
example.en: See you at eight? OK, perfect.

words.note: Enthusiastic yes: "¿Vamos? —¡De una!". Informal, very common among young people.

example.es: —¿Pedimos pizza? —¡De una, me muero de hambre!
example.en: —Shall we order pizza? —Sure, I'm really hungry!

words.note: Very common instead of "otra vez".

example.es: No te entendí, ¿me lo decís de vuelta?
example.en: I didn't get it, can you say it again?

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials VI
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Surprise, a warning, or a playful compliment.

example.es: ¡Epa, qué elegante que viniste hoy!
example.en: Wow, you look so elegant today!

words.note: Intensifier before a noun: "flor de quilombo" is a huge mess, "flor de asado" a great barbecue.

example.es: Nos comimos flor de asado el domingo.
example.en: We had a great barbecue on Sunday.

words.note: A bad or annoying situation. "¡Qué garrón!" means what a drag.

example.es: Qué garrón, se suspendió el recital.
example.en: What a shame, the concert got canceled.

words.note: Literally a great goal. Used for any great news: "¡Golazo!".

example.es: ¿Conseguiste el laburo? ¡Golazo!
example.en: You got the job? Awesome!

words.note: "Es un grupo" means it's made up. A "grupero" is someone who makes stuff up.

example.es: Eso es puro grupo, no le creas.
example.en: That's all lies, don't believe him.

packs.name: Essentials VII
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials VII
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Means great or perfect. "Joya" alone answers "sounds good".

example.es: —Nos vemos a las ocho. —¡Joya!
example.en: "See you at eight." "Great!"

words.note: Closes a deal or topic: "listo, nos vemos mañana". Also "¿listo?" to check agreement. Everyday word.

example.es: Listo, entonces paso a buscarte a las siete.
example.en: Okay, so I'll pick you up at seven.

words.note: Reaction to news, real or feigned surprise: "¡Mirá vos!". Can sound ironic with a flat tone.

example.es: —Se casa Martín. —¡Mirá vos! No sabía que tenía novia.
example.en: —Martín is getting married. —Well, look at that! I didn't know he had a girlfriend.

words.note: That has nothing to do with it, or "not at all" as a reply. "Es re nada que ver": it's totally off.

example.es: ¿Que yo estoy enojado? Nada que ver, estoy cansado.
example.en: Me, angry? Not at all, I'm tired.

words.note: Strong denial: no way, not even close. Also "ni ahí con eso": not into it. Informal.

example.es: Ni ahí voy a esa fiesta, no conozco a nadie.
example.en: No way am I going to that party, I don't know anyone.

packs.name: Essentials VIII
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials VIII
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: "No da" means it's not appropriate or not worth it: "no da ir así vestido". Informal.

example.es: No da llegar tarde a la entrevista, salgamos ya.
example.en: It's not cool to be late to the interview, let's leave.

words.note: The go-to "of course" in Argentina: "¡Obvio!" or "obvio que sí". Informal but used by everyone.

example.es: —¿Venís al asado? —¡Obvio! ¿Qué llevo?
example.en: —Are you coming to the barbecue? —Of course! What should I bring?

words.note: "¡Qué paja!" means what a drag; "me da paja" is I can't be bothered. Also slang for masturbation.

example.es: Me da paja salir con este frío.
example.en: I don't feel like going out in this cold.

words.note: Something silly or trivial. "¡No digas pavadas!" means don't talk nonsense.

example.es: Se pelearon por una pavada.
example.en: They fought over nothing.

words.note: Low-quality or disappointing. From "pedo", fart, but used casually by everyone.

example.es: La peli era re pedorra, me dormí.
example.en: The movie was so bad, I fell asleep.

packs.name: Essentials IX
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials IX
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Cool, easygoing or clever. "Un tipo piola" is a good guy; "quedate piola" means keep quiet, lay low.

example.es: Tu amigo es re piola, me cayó muy bien.
example.en: Your friend is really cool, I liked him a lot.

words.note: Filler meaning "let's say" or "sort of"; also "yeah, sure" when unconvinced.

example.es: Llegamos a las nueve, ponele.
example.en: We'll get there around nine, let's say.

words.note: "Posta" means for real, truly. "¿Posta?" is really? "La posta" is the real deal.

example.es: ¿Posta que te vas a vivir a España?
example.en: Are you seriously moving to Spain?

words.note: Mild, polite way to show disappointment or sympathy. Often "¡la pucha!". A softened form of a ruder word, fine to say anywhere.

example.es: Pucha, no llegué a tiempo para el colectivo.
example.en: Oh no, I didn't make it in time for the bus.

packs.name: Essentials X
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials X
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Casual greeting, or "¿qué onda con...?" to ask what's going on with something. Informal.

example.es: ¿Qué onda, che? ¿Salimos esta noche?
example.en: What's up? Are we going out tonight?

words.note: Shrugging filler when unsure or vague. Often at the end: "...y qué sé yo". Neutral, everyone says it.

example.es: No sé, podemos ir al cine, al parque, qué sé yo.
example.en: I don't know, we could go to the movies, the park, whatever.

words.note: Everywhere in Argentine speech. Goes before adjectives and verbs: "re lindo", "me re gustó". "Re que sí" = totally.

example.es: La película estuvo re buena, te va a encantar.
example.en: The movie was really good, you're going to love it.

words.note: Without fail, one way or another: "tenés que venir sí o sí". Neutral, everyone uses it.

example.es: El viernes tenemos que terminar esto sí o sí.
example.en: We have to finish this by Friday no matter what.

words.note: Total agreement: "¡Tal cual!", that's exactly it. Informal and very frequent.

example.es: —Este país es una montaña rusa. —Tal cual.
example.en: —This country is a roller coaster. —Exactly.

packs.name: Essentials XI
packs.title: Everyday talk · Essentials XI
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Filler like English "like": "tipo, no sé". Also means around with times: "tipo ocho", around eight.

example.es: Nos vemos tipo nueve en la puerta del bar.
example.en: See you around nine at the bar door.

words.note: "¿Todo bien?" is a standard greeting; "todo bien" also means no problem or it's fine.

example.es: Hola, che, ¿todo bien? Hace mil que no te veo.
example.en: Hey, all good? I haven't seen you in ages.

words.note: Shows annoyance or boredom, like a sigh. Kids say it a lot, adults too.

example.es: ¡Ufa! Otra vez se cortó la luz.
example.en: Ugh! The power went out again.

words.note: A little, briefly: "esperá un toque", "un toque de sal". Softens requests. Informal.

example.es: Esperame un toque que termino y salimos.
example.en: Wait a sec, I'll finish and we'll head out.

words.note: A lot: "te quiero una banda", "había una banda de gente". Informal, very common.

example.es: Había una banda de gente en la cancha.
example.en: There were a lot of people at the stadium.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Everyday talk · Everyday
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: From "ver". Tag at the end or middle of a sentence: "¿viste?". Porteños use it constantly.

example.es: Estaba re cansado, ¿viste?, y me fui temprano.
example.en: I was really tired, you know, so I left early.

words.note: Whatever, it's done, let it go. Also to decide on impulse: "ya fue, me lo compro".

example.es: Ya fue, no me contestó. Me voy a dormir.
example.en: Forget it, he didn't answer. I'm going to bed.

words.note: Something or someone out of line or wild. Also "awesome": "un recital zarpado". Context tells you which.

example.es: Lo que dijo fue re zarpado, todos se quedaron callados.
example.en: What he said was really rude, everyone went quiet.

words.note: Opening word of the classic lullaby every Argentine knows: "Arrorró mi niño, arrorró mi sol".

example.es: Arrorró mi niño, arrorró mi sol, arrorró pedazo de mi corazón.
example.en: Sleep, my baby, sleep, my sun, sleep, piece of my heart.

words.note: From Italian "attenti". Playful way to say pay attention.

example.es: Atenti, que viene el jefe.
example.en: Watch out, the boss is coming.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Everyday talk · Going deeper I
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: "Sos boleta": you're dead meat, as a threat or joke. As a noun, "boleta" is a ballot or a bill.

example.es: Si mamá ve el auto rayado, sos boleta.
example.en: If mom sees the car scratched, you're in big trouble.

words.note: "Una chorrera de" means loads of something.

example.es: Tengo una chorrera de mails sin contestar.
example.en: I have a lot of unanswered emails.

words.note: Excellent, a ten out of ten: "quedó de diez". Casual and positive.

example.es: La comida estuvo de diez, gracias por invitarnos.
example.en: The food was perfect, thanks for inviting us.

words.note: Enthusiastic agreement among young people: "—¿Vamos? —¡De más!". Informal.

example.es: —¿Te copa ir a la costa? —¡De más!
example.en: —Want to go to the coast? —Of course!

words.note: Said of a situation or a person that is hard to deal with. "Se puso espesa la cosa" means things got tense.

example.es: La reunión se puso espesa cuando hablaron de plata.
example.en: The meeting got tense when they talked about money.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Everyday talk · Going deeper II
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: "Es fija": it's certain, it'll happen for sure. From horse-racing slang. Informal.

example.es: Si llueve, es fija que el subte se llena.
example.en: If it rains, it's a sure thing the subway fills up.

words.note: Something rude or vulgar said or done.

example.es: Dejá de decir guarangadas delante de mi vieja.
example.en: Stop saying rude things in front of my mom.

words.note: Messy or careless work. Prolijo means neat, a very Argentine word.

example.es: El trabajo está bien, pero es muy improlijo.
example.en: The work is fine, but it's really messy.

words.note: Youth slang intensifier after a verb: "me gusta mal" means I really love it. Mainly teens and twenty-somethings.

example.es: Ese tema me gusta mal, lo escucho todo el día.
example.en: I really love that song, I play it all day.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Everyday talk · Going deeper III
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: A fun word for a chaotic mess or fuss. Playful, used by all ages.

example.es: Se armó un merequetengue bárbaro en la reunión de consorcio.
example.en: There was a big mess at the building meeting.

words.note: A cheeky "no way!" or "forget it!". Casual, a bit cheeky but not a swear word.

example.es: ¿Que te preste el auto? ¡Minga!
example.en: Lend you my car? No way!

words.note: "¡Olvidate!" means absolutely, count on it, not forget it. Context decides; tone is enthusiastic.

example.es: —¿Me ayudás con la mudanza? —¡Olvidate! Ahí estoy.
example.en: —Will you help me move? —Of course! I'll be there.

words.note: "¡Opa!" for surprise or when something almost falls. Also "upa" when lifting a kid.

example.es: ¡Opa! Casi se te cae el vaso.
example.en: Oops! You almost dropped the glass.

words.note: A mistake or miss. The verb "pifiar" is to get it wrong.

example.es: Fue un pifie mío, mandé el mail a otra persona.
example.en: My mistake, I sent the email to someone else.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: Everyday talk · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Fillers, reactions and the little words every conversation runs on.

words.note: Only for age: "tiene cuarenta pirulos" means he's forty. Jokey.

example.es: Mi viejo ya tiene setenta pirulos.
example.en: My dad is already seventy years old.

words.note: "¡Qué plato!" means how hilarious. Said of a funny situation or person.

example.es: Tu tío disfrazado de Papá Noel fue un plato.
example.en: Your uncle dressed up as Santa was so funny.

words.note: "¡Sonaste!" warns someone they're in trouble. From "sonar", to be doomed. Jokey or serious.

example.es: Si tu vieja ve esa nota, sonaste.
example.en: If your mom sees that grade, you're in trouble.

words.note: Short for tranquilo: "todo tranca", everything's calm. Also "tranca" as reassurance: relax. Informal.

example.es: Tranca, no pasa nada, lo arreglamos mañana.
example.en: Relax, it's no big deal, we'll fix it tomorrow.

words.note: "No le des calce": don't give them an opening. Used for flirting or arguments.

example.es: Si le das calce, no te deja en paz.
example.en: If you give him a chance, he won't leave you alone.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: People · Essentials I
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Blend of "amigo" and "novio". Someone you hook up with but aren't officially dating.

example.es: No es mi novio, es un amigovio nomás.
example.en: He's not my boyfriend, just a friend with benefits.

words.note: Informal word for a band's drummer, from "batería".

example.es: El batero de la banda es amigo mío.
example.en: The band's drummer is a friend of mine.

words.note: A very smart person. "Bocho" also means head: "me duele el bocho".

example.es: Preguntale a Juli, que es un bocho en matemática.
example.en: Ask Juli, she's a genius at math.

words.note: Very common word for a tattletale or informer.

example.es: ¿Quién fue el buchón que le contó a la vieja?
example.en: Who was the traitor who told mom?

words.note: The police, or a cop. "Ir en cana": to go to jail. "Caer en cana": to get caught.

example.es: ¡Rajemos, que viene la cana!
example.en: Let's run, the cops are coming!

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: People · Essentials II
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Someone self-assured and street-smart, sometimes a bit cocky. Very common.

example.es: Se hace el canchero, pero está re nervioso.
example.en: He acts all cool, but he is really nervous.

words.note: Someone great at something or just a great person. "Sos un capo" is high praise, often a thank-you.

example.es: Me arreglaste la compu, sos un capo.
example.en: You fixed my computer, you're the best.

words.note: Someone who doesn't drink or do drugs, or who acts fake and proper. Mildly mocking.

example.es: No seas careta y quedate un rato más.
example.en: Don't be so boring, stay a bit longer.

words.note: Very common for any guy. Feminine: "chabona".

example.es: ¿Viste al chabón que atiende el kiosco? Es re buena onda.
example.en: Did you see the guy at the kiosk? He's really nice.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: People · Essentials III
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Someone who flirts or talks their way out of things with nice words.

example.es: No le creas nada, es un chamuyero bárbaro.
example.en: Don't believe a word, he's a big liar.

words.note: A bluffer or con man who promises and doesn't deliver.

example.es: El plomero es un chanta: cobró y nunca vino.
example.en: The plumber is a cheat: he got paid and never came.

words.note: Snobby, upper-class. Can be a noun: "los chetos de Recoleta".

example.es: Es un bar muy cheto, una cerveza sale una fortuna.
example.en: It's a really fancy bar, a beer costs a fortune.

words.note: Everyday word for a thief. Also used for corrupt politicians.

example.es: Agarraron al chorro que robaba en la plaza.
example.en: They caught the thief who was robbing people in the square.

words.note: A nosy person who gossips. Also an adjective: "¡qué chusma!".

example.es: Mi vecina es re chusma, sabe todo de todos.
example.en: My neighbor is such a gossip, she knows everything about everyone.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: People · Essentials IV
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Driver of a "colectivo", the city bus. Famous for fast driving and not stopping.

example.es: El colectivero no paró y me dejó en la parada.
example.en: The bus driver didn't stop and left me at the stop.

words.note: The world of TV celebrities and gossip. Often a bit dismissive.

example.es: No miro programas de farándula, me aburren.
example.en: I don't watch celebrity gossip shows, they bore me.

words.note: Used to address a guy you don't know, often a bit brusque. Also means a young man.

example.es: Pará, flaco, yo estaba primero en la fila.
example.en: Hold on, man, I was first in line.

words.note: Loving nickname for a partner, friend or kid. Has nothing to do with weight. Also "gordo" and "gorda".

example.es: Gordi, ¿me pasás a buscar a la salida del laburo?
example.en: Honey, can you pick me up after work?

words.note: Great, impressive; for people and things. "Es un groso" is a big compliment. Also spelled "grosso".

example.es: Tu viejo es un groso, nos llevó a todos al aeropuerto.
example.en: Your dad is awesome, he drove us all to the airport.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: People · Essentials V
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Friendly way to address a guy, like "man" or "dude": "¿Qué hacés, loco?". Informal.

example.es: ¿Qué hacés, loco? Tanto tiempo.
example.en: What's up, man? Long time no see.

words.note: Very common casual word for a woman. Lunfardo; not rude among friends, but informal.

example.es: Esa mina trabaja conmigo en la oficina.
example.en: That woman works with me at the office.

words.note: A mild, almost friendly insult, like "dummy". Literally a turnip.

example.es: ¡Qué nabo que soy, me olvidé las llaves adentro!
example.en: I'm such an idiot, I left my keys inside!

words.note: From Italian "nonna", used by millions of Argentines of Italian descent. "Nono" is grandpa.

example.es: Los domingos comemos ñoquis en lo de la nona.
example.en: On Sundays we eat gnocchi at grandma's.

words.note: In Argentina it means a kid or teenager, often dismissive. Rude in Mexico, careful.

example.es: Unos pendejos estaban jodiendo en la plaza.
example.en: Some kids were messing around in the square.

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: People · Essentials VI
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Feminine of "pibe": a girl or young woman. Also "la piba" for a girlfriend.

example.es: Conocí a una piba re copada en la facu.
example.en: I met a really cool girl at college.

words.note: The classic word for a boy or young guy. "El pibe" can also mean one's boyfriend.

example.es: Ese pibe juega bárbaro a la pelota.
example.en: That kid plays football great.

words.note: Someone from the city of Buenos Aires, from "puerto". Also an adjective.

example.es: Los porteños siempre andan apurados.
example.en: People from Buenos Aires are always in a hurry.

words.note: Literally salami. A mild, almost affectionate insult, often said among friends or to kids.

example.es: No seas salame, fijate antes de cruzar la calle.
example.en: Don't be an idiot, look before you cross the street.

packs.name: Essentials VII
packs.title: People · Essentials VII
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: How kids address and talk about their female teacher, short for señorita. "La seño" of kindergarten or primary school.

example.es: La seño nos dejó tarea para el lunes.
example.en: Our teacher gave us homework for Monday.

words.note: A taxi driver; the taxi itself is a "tacho". Informal, very porteño.

example.es: El tachero me contó toda su vida en diez cuadras.
example.en: The taxi driver told me his whole life in ten blocks.

words.note: Short for napolitano. Friendly, very common: many Argentines have Italian grandparents, and "el Tano" is a classic nickname.

example.es: Mi abuelo era tano y hacía los ñoquis caseros.
example.en: My grandpa was Italian and made homemade gnocchi.

words.note: Nickname for Martín, turned into the stereotype of a preppy rich guy: rugby, loafers, sweater over shoulders.

example.es: El bar se llenó de tinchos con camisa celeste.
example.en: The bar filled up with rich guys in light-blue shirts.

words.note: Affectionate, not rude: "mi vieja" is my mom, "mi viejo" my dad, "mis viejos" my parents.

example.es: Este domingo como en lo de mi vieja.
example.en: This Sunday I'm eating at my mom's.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: People · Going deeper I
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Full of himself, acting bigger than he is. "Se agrandó" means he got cocky.

example.es: Desde que lo ascendieron está re agrandado.
example.en: Since he got promoted he's been really arrogant.

words.note: Once a bum or vagrant; now mostly an affectionate word for a cheeky, shameless person.

example.es: Tu sobrino es un atorrante, se comió todas las facturas.
example.en: Your nephew is so naughty, he ate all the pastries.

words.note: "Hacerse el banana": to act cocky or smart. Also the fruit; Argentines never say "plátano".

example.es: No te hagas el banana, que te conozco.
example.en: Don't act so clever, I know you.

words.note: Someone who rats people out. In old lunfardo it also meant a cop.

example.es: No le cuentes nada, que es un botón.
example.en: Don't tell him anything, he tells everyone.

words.note: Someone who collects cardboard and recyclables from the street to sell. A common sight since 2001.

example.es: A la noche pasan los cartoneros por la cuadra.
example.en: At night the cardboard collectors come down the block.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: People · Going deeper II
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: "Tener chapa" means having status or reputation. Also sheet metal, as in "techo de chapa".

example.es: Ese abogado tiene chapa, lo conocen en todos los juzgados.
example.en: That lawyer has influence, every court knows him.

words.note: Someone who lives off collecting trash. Also a scruffy person, jokingly.

example.es: Con esa ropa parecés un ciruja.
example.en: In those clothes you look like a homeless person.

words.note: Posh and snobby, a stronger version of "cheto".

example.es: Va a un colegio concheto de San Isidro.
example.en: He goes to a fancy school in San Isidro.

words.note: The presenter of a TV or radio show. Also a driver.

example.es: El conductor del programa hizo una pregunta incómoda.
example.en: The show's host asked an awkward question.

words.note: Short for "compañero". Also used in political circles.

example.es: Vamos con los cumpas a la marcha del sábado.
example.en: We're going to Saturday's march with my friends.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: People · Going deeper III
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Young couples celebrate each month together.

example.es: Hoy es nuestro cumplemés y me regaló flores.
example.en: Today is our month anniversary and he gave me flowers.

words.note: Crazy or out of control, in a funny way.

example.es: Tu primo está medio deschavetado, se tiró al río vestido.
example.en: Your cousin is a bit crazy, he jumped in the river with his clothes on.

words.note: Someone who approaches people directly, especially to flirt.

example.es: Es muy encarador, le habla a cualquiera en el boliche.
example.en: He's really bold, he talks to anyone at the club.

words.note: Friendly and easy to get along with, good at charming people.

example.es: El nuevo es muy entrador, ya se hizo amigo de todos.
example.en: The new guy is really outgoing, he's friends with everyone already.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: People · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Short for fanático: a big fan of a band, team or show. Same form for men and women.

example.es: Soy re fana de Soda Stereo desde chica.
example.en: I've been a huge Soda Stereo fan since I was a girl.

words.note: Someone visibly wrecked by partying and drugs. Joking between friends, insulting otherwise.

example.es: Después de tres noches sin dormir estaba hecho un fisura.
example.en: After three nights without sleep he was a total mess.

words.note: Tacky or low-class in taste, like "mersa". Snobbish; used for people, clothes or music.

example.es: Esa camisa brillante es medio grasa, ¿no?
example.en: That shiny shirt is kind of ugly, isn't it?

words.note: Someone ill-mannered or vulgar.

example.es: No seas guarango y saludá a tu tía.
example.en: Don't be rude, say hi to your aunt.

words.note: The man with the sack who takes children who misbehave.

example.es: Si no te dormís, viene el hombre de la bolsa.
example.en: If you don't go to sleep, the monster will come.

packs.name: Going deeper V
packs.title: People · Going deeper V
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Person who runs a kiosco, the tiny shop selling candy, smokes and drinks. Often knows the whole block.

example.es: El kiosquero de la esquina me fía los alfajores.
example.en: The guy at the corner kiosk lets me buy alfajores on credit.

words.note: A homeless drifter. Said to come from the Italian for bundle.

example.es: Un linyera dormía en el banco de la plaza.
example.en: A homeless man was sleeping on the park bench.

words.note: Tacky or gaudy, for things or people. Similar to "grasa". Slightly old-fashioned but everyone knows it.

example.es: Ese auto dorado es re mersa.
example.en: That gold car is so ugly.

words.note: Masculine of "mina": a man, often a good-looking one. Casual.

example.es: ¿Viste al mino nuevo del gimnasio?
example.en: Did you see the new handsome guy at the gym?

words.note: Street slang for a friend, from "compañero". Also used for a rough, streetwise guy.

example.es: Vino con todos sus ñeris del barrio.
example.en: He came with all his buddies from the neighborhood.

packs.name: Going deeper VI
packs.title: People · Going deeper VI
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: Literally "French fry": a mild, funny way to call someone a fool.

example.es: No seas papa frita, llevate el paraguas.
example.en: Don't be silly, take the umbrella.

words.note: A group of guys who bully or attack together. "Patotero" is one of them.

example.es: Una patota le pegó a un pibe a la salida.
example.en: A gang beat up a kid outside.

words.note: Cheap, tight with money. A bit old-school but understood.

example.es: No seas pijotero y dejale propina al mozo.
example.en: Don't be stingy, leave the waiter a tip.

words.note: A boring or tiresome person, heavy as lead. "¡Qué plomo!" also works for a dull thing.

example.es: El novio de mi hermana es un plomo, habla solo de impuestos.
example.en: My sister's boyfriend is so boring, he only talks about taxes.

words.note: An attractive person, literally a colt. "Está hecho un potro."

example.es: Tu primo está hecho un potro.
example.en: Your cousin is really handsome now.

packs.name: Going deeper VII
packs.title: People · Going deeper VII
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: A rugby player, and the stereotype of the posh, macho private-school guy. Often said with disdain.

example.es: En esa fiesta había puros rugbiers de colegio privado.
example.en: That party was full of private-school rugby guys.

words.note: A student who studies all the time, a bookworm. Teasing, not harsh. "Es re traga".

example.es: Sos un traga, ya leíste todo el apunte.
example.en: You're such a nerd, you already read all the notes.

words.note: Guy who "watches" parked cars on the street for a tip, waving a rag. Usually unofficial.

example.es: El trapito me pidió quinientos pesos para cuidar el auto.
example.en: The street parking guy asked me for five hundred pesos.

words.note: Someone who makes a fuss, hesitates or beats around the bush. "No seas vueltero" = just decide.

example.es: No seas vueltero y elegí un restaurante de una vez.
example.en: Don't be so indecisive and just pick a restaurant already.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: People · Rare gems
packs.about: Kids, friends, cops, posh people and everyone in between.

words.note: From "afanar", to steal, which is much more common. Informal.

example.es: Cuidado con el celu, que ese tipo es un afanador.
example.en: Careful with your phone, that guy is a thief.

words.note: Moody and easily annoyed. From "chinche", to get upset. Informal.

example.es: Mi abuelo se levanta chinchudo si no toma mate.
example.en: My grandpa wakes up in a bad mood if he doesn't have his mate.

words.note: Argentine word for an undertaker or funeral-home worker. The funeral home itself is a "cochería".

example.es: El funebrero llegó a las ocho para organizar todo.
example.en: The funeral worker arrived at eight to organize everything.

words.note: Common in the Litoral and Uruguay. Plural gurises; a girl is a gurisa.

example.es: Los gurises están jugando en el patio.
example.en: The kids are playing in the yard.

words.note: Originally an indigenous raid. "Caer en malón" is to show up as a big group.

example.es: Cayeron en malón a casa y se comieron todo.
example.en: They came to my place in a big group and ate everything.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Money & work · Essentials I
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: Someone who got a job through connections, not merit. Very common complaint about public jobs.

example.es: Ese no sabe nada, entró de acomodado por el tío.
example.en: That guy knows nothing, he got in through his uncle.

words.note: The legally required extra half-month salary paid in June and December. Everyone waits for it.

example.es: Con el aguinaldo de diciembre me voy de vacaciones.
example.en: With the December bonus I'm going on vacation.

words.note: The easy word-based name of a bank or wallet account, used for instant transfers. "Pasame el alias".

example.es: Pasame tu alias y te transfiero lo del asado.
example.en: Send me your account alias and I'll transfer the barbecue money.

words.note: Black-market dollar dealers on Florida street who stand still calling "cambio, cambio" like trees.

example.es: Le cambié los dólares a un arbolito en la calle Florida.
example.en: I changed my dollars with a street changer on Florida.

words.note: Literally "little pig". Also a term of affection.

example.es: Rompí el chanchito para comprarme la bici.
example.en: I broke my piggy bank to buy the bike.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Money & work · Essentials II
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: A small, informal paid job. "Hacer changas" is doing gigs to get by.

example.es: Este mes vivo de changas hasta que consiga algo fijo.
example.en: This month I live from temporary jobs until I find a stable job.

words.note: Where people buy dólar blue, often a hidden office downtown.

example.es: Cambié los dólares en una cueva de la calle Florida.
example.en: I changed my dollars at an illegal exchange on Florida Street.

words.note: Paying by card in monthly installments at no extra cost. A national habit: "¿en cuántas cuotas?".

example.es: Me compré la heladera en doce cuotas sin interés.
example.en: I bought the fridge in twelve interest-free payments.

words.note: A shady business or scam. "Es un curro" means it's a rip-off.

example.es: Eso de cobrar por la bolsa es un curro.
example.en: Charging for the bag is a scam.

words.note: The unofficial dollar rate, followed daily on the news.

example.es: ¿A cuánto está el dólar blue hoy?
example.en: What's the black-market dollar rate today?

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Money & work · Essentials III
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: Work or pay not declared to the tax office. The opposite is "en blanco".

example.es: Trabajo en negro, así que no tengo obra social.
example.en: I work without a contract, so I have no health insurance.

words.note: A work day off in a rotating schedule. "Estar de franco": to be off work.

example.es: Mañana estoy de franco, así que podemos juntarnos.
example.en: I have the day off tomorrow, so we can meet.

words.note: Very common slang for money.

example.es: No tengo guita para salir este finde.
example.en: I don't have any cash to go out this weekend.

words.note: A working person, with pride: "soy laburante".

example.es: Es un laburante, se levanta a las cinco todos los días.
example.en: He's a hard worker, he gets up at five every day.

words.note: From Italian lavoro. The everyday word for work or job.

example.es: Consiguió un laburo nuevo en el centro.
example.en: He got a new job downtown.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Money & work · Essentials IV
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: A thousand pesos. "Diez lucas" is ten thousand.

example.es: Me salió diez lucas la cena.
example.en: The dinner cost me ten thousand pesos.

words.note: Lunfardo for a peso or money in general. "No tengo un mango" means I'm broke.

example.es: No tengo un mango hasta que cobre el sueldo.
example.en: I don't have a peso until I get paid.

words.note: Union-run health insurance tied to your job. Private plans are "prepagas".

example.es: Mi obra social no cubre el dentista.
example.en: My health insurance doesn't cover the dentist.

words.note: Informal for one million, usually pesos: "dos palos". "Palo verde" is a million dollars.

example.es: Se compró un auto usado por diez palos.
example.en: He bought a used car for ten million.

words.note: Informal: something is expensive. "Está salado" is what you say when you see a price that hurts.

example.es: Me gusta la campera, pero está re salada.
example.en: I like the jacket, but it's really expensive.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Money & work · Everyday
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: The money you get back after paying. In Spain it's "la vuelta". "Quedate con el vuelto": keep the change.

example.es: Quedate con el vuelto, está todo bien.
example.en: Keep the change, it's all good.

words.note: To get yourself a comfortable position, usually through connections. Also to become well-off.

example.es: Se acomodó en el ministerio y no labura nunca.
example.en: He got an easy job at the ministry and never works.

words.note: Someone paid by the job to carry or load things, at markets or ports.

example.es: Contratamos a un changarín para bajar la heladera.
example.en: We hired a day worker to carry the fridge downstairs.

words.note: Informal: having no money at all. Also "estar seco" or "estar en la lona".

example.es: No puedo salir hoy, estoy pato hasta que cobre.
example.en: I can't go out today, I have no money until I get paid.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Money & work · Going deeper I
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: A holiday added to join a public holiday to the weekend, creating a long weekend or "finde largo".

example.es: Con el feriado puente nos vamos cuatro días a la costa.
example.en: With the long weekend we're going to the coast for four days.

words.note: Playful form of gratis.

example.es: La entrada es gratarola, vamos.
example.en: Entry is free, let's go.

words.note: The person who washes dishes in a restaurant. A classic first job.

example.es: Empecé como lavacopas en un restaurante de Palermo.
example.en: I started as a dishwasher at a restaurant in Palermo.

words.note: Someone paying the simplified "monotributo" tax, i.e. a self-employed freelancer.

example.es: Soy monotributista, así que te hago factura C.
example.en: I'm self-employed, so I'll give you a type C invoice.

words.note: The yearly collective bargaining between unions and employers over salaries. Usually plural: "las paritarias".

example.es: Cerraron la paritaria y nos aumentan un diez por ciento.
example.en: They signed the salary agreement and our pay goes up ten percent.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Money & work · Going deeper II
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: A bank term deposit, the classic Argentine way to earn interest on pesos for 30 days.

example.es: Puse el aguinaldo en un plazo fijo a treinta días.
example.en: I put my bonus in a 30-day fixed-term deposit.

words.note: The card terminal in shops, named after a brand. "¿Tenés posnet?" asks if they take cards.

example.es: Perdón, no tenemos posnet, solo efectivo o transferencia.
example.en: Sorry, we have no card machine, only cash or bank transfer.

words.note: Any way of making extra money on the side, often improvised. "Vivir del rebusque": getting by on odd jobs.

example.es: Vendo tortas los findes, es mi rebusque.
example.en: I sell cakes on weekends, it's my extra job.

words.note: To pay part in advance to reserve something. The deposit itself is "la seña".

example.es: Ya señamos el salón para el cumple de la nena.
example.en: We already paid a deposit on the party room for our daughter's birthday.

words.note: "Un toco" means a lot, usually of money: "un toco de plata". Also a big chunk of something.

example.es: Ese auto le salió un toco de guita.
example.en: That car cost him a lot of money.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Money & work · Rare gems
packs.about: Cash, jobs, prices and getting by.

words.note: Pooling money among friends to pay for something: "hacer una vaquita" or "hacer vaca".

example.es: Hagamos una vaquita para el regalo de Sofi.
example.en: Let's all put in money for Sofi's present.

words.note: To save up and hold on to money tightly. Related: "amarrete", a stingy person.

example.es: Amarrocó dólares durante años para comprarse el depto.
example.en: He saved dollars for years to buy his apartment.

words.note: Money hidden away for emergencies. "Tener un canuto" or "hacer un canuto".

example.es: Tengo un canuto de dólares guardado en el placard.
example.en: I have some dollars hidden in the closet.

words.note: Slang for paying, like pulling the trigger on your wallet.

example.es: Al final me tocó gatillar la cuenta del bar.
example.en: In the end I had to pay the bill at the bar.

words.note: To haggle over small amounts or penny-pinch. A "pichulero" is a cheapskate.

example.es: No le pichulees al verdulero por diez pesos.
example.en: Don't argue with the vegetable seller over ten pesos.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials I
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Grilled organ meats at an asado: chinchulines, mollejas, riñones. Usually plural.

example.es: Yo arranco siempre con las achuras y un chori.
example.en: I always start with the organ meat and a sausage.

words.note: The Argentine word; "alcachofa" in most places.

example.es: Compré alcauciles en la verdulería para hacer al vapor.
example.en: I bought artichokes at the vegetable shop to steam.

words.note: Two soft cookies with dulce de leche, often chocolate-coated. Sold in every kiosco.

example.es: Me compré un alfajor en el kiosco para el viaje.
example.en: I bought a filled cookie at the kiosk for the trip.

words.note: The Argentine word; most countries say "piña". Plural "ananás".

example.es: ¿Le ponés ananá a la pizza? ¡Estás loco!
example.en: You put pineapple on pizza? You're crazy!

words.note: Both the grilled meat and the social event around it. "Hacer un asado" is a weekend ritual.

example.es: El domingo hacemos un asado en lo de mi viejo.
example.en: On Sunday we're having a barbecue at my dad's.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials II
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: The Argentine word. "Dulce de batata" with cheese is the classic "postre vigilante".

example.es: Hice batatas al horno para acompañar el pollo.
example.en: I made roasted sweet potatoes to go with the chicken.

words.note: A thick steak from the sirloin, the steakhouse star. Nothing to do with chorizo sausage.

example.es: Pedí un bife de chorizo jugoso con ensalada.
example.en: I ordered a juicy steak with salad.

words.note: The basic home-made cake, often filled with dulce de leche for birthdays.

example.es: Mi abuela hace un bizcochuelo de naranja buenísimo.
example.en: My grandma makes a great orange sponge cake.

words.note: Pork neck or shoulder, grilled at asados or cured like a cold cut. "Sánguche de bondiola" is a classic.

example.es: Hicimos bondiola a la parrilla con salsa de mostaza.
example.en: We grilled pork shoulder with mustard sauce.

words.note: What Argentines call cashews. Spain says "anacardo".

example.es: Compré castañas de cajú para picar con la cerveza.
example.en: I bought cashews to eat with the beer.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials III
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: The person who prepares and passes around the mate in a group.

example.es: Hoy el cebador soy yo, pasame el termo.
example.en: I'm serving the mate today, pass me the thermos.

words.note: Scallions. You'll see it on menus and at the verdulería.

example.es: Le puse cebolla de verdeo a la tortilla.
example.en: I put green onion in the Spanish omelet.

words.note: Also "dos chauchas": peanuts, a tiny amount of money, as in "gana dos chauchas".

example.es: Hice una ensalada de chauchas con huevo.
example.en: I made a green bean salad with egg.

words.note: Oil, vinegar, garlic, parsley, oregano and chili flakes. The standard sauce for grilled meat.

example.es: Pasame el chimichurri para el choripán.
example.en: Pass me the herb sauce for the sausage sandwich.

words.note: Small cheesy rolls made with cassava starch, from Guaraní cooking.

example.es: Compramos chipá calentito en la estación.
example.en: We bought warm cheese bread at the station.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials IV
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: A small chocolate bar from the kiosk. "Jack" is a famous brand.

example.es: Me compré un chocolatín en el kiosco.
example.en: I bought myself a chocolate bar at the kiosk.

words.note: Grilled chorizo in bread, a classic at asados and outside stadiums.

example.es: A la salida de la cancha nos comimos un choripán.
example.en: After the game we ate a chorizo sandwich.

words.note: A crunchy tube filled with dulce de leche, often dipped in chocolate.

example.es: En la plaza vendían cubanitos de dulce de leche.
example.en: They were selling dulce de leche wafer rolls in the square.

words.note: The national sweet: milk and sugar cooked down. On toast, in alfajores, in everything.

example.es: Me comí medio pote de dulce de leche a cucharadas.
example.en: I ate half a jar of milk caramel by the spoonful.

words.note: Sweet pastries from the bakery, like medialunas, bought by the dozen for mate time.

example.es: Traé una docena de facturas para el mate.
example.en: Bring a dozen pastries to go with the mate.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials V
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Italian bitter drunk almost only with Coca-Cola, hugely popular, especially in Córdoba. "Un fernet con coca".

example.es: Prepará un fernet con coca para la previa.
example.en: Make a fernet and Coke for before the party.

words.note: A thin slice of cheese, ham or cold cuts. Elsewhere people say loncha or rebanada.

example.es: Poneme dos fetas de jamón en el sánguche.
example.en: Put two slices of ham in my sandwich.

words.note: Used in Argentina instead of "fresa". "Frutillas con crema" is a classic dessert.

example.es: De postre hay frutillas con crema.
example.en: For dessert there are strawberries with cream.

words.note: Any soft drink. "Refresco" is rarely heard in Argentina.

example.es: ¿Querés agua o gaseosa con la pizza?
example.en: Do you want water or soda with the pizza?

words.note: Creamy corn cooked with onion, from the northwest. Empanadas de humita are a classic.

example.es: Pedí media docena de empanadas de humita.
example.en: I ordered half a dozen corn empanadas.

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials VI
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Cured ham. Jamón alone usually means cooked ham.

example.es: Armamos una picada con jamón crudo y queso.
example.en: We made a snack plate with cured ham and cheese.

words.note: Fruit blended with milk or water. Licuado de banana is the classic.

example.es: Me tomé un licuado de banana con leche.
example.en: I had a banana milk smoothie.

words.note: What Argentines say for butter; "mantequilla" sounds foreign. "Tirar manteca al techo" means to splash money around.

example.es: ¿Me pasás la manteca para las tostadas?
example.en: Can you pass me the butter for the toast?

words.note: Yerba infusion sipped through a bombilla and passed around a group. "¿Tomamos unos mates?"

example.es: ¿Querés un mate o preferís un café?
example.en: Want some mate or would you rather have coffee?

words.note: To sit and share mate, usually slowly and with conversation. Very common.

example.es: Los domingos nos juntamos a matear en la plaza.
example.en: On Sundays we get together to drink mate in the park.

packs.name: Essentials VII
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials VII
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Smaller and sweeter than a French croissant; "de manteca" is sweet, "de grasa" is savory.

example.es: Traé una docena de medialunas para el mate.
example.en: Bring a dozen croissants for the mate.

words.note: Slang for "milanesa", the breaded cutlet Argentines adore. Casual and affectionate.

example.es: Hoy hay milanga con puré, ¿te quedás a comer?
example.en: There's breaded steak and mashed potatoes today, are you staying to eat?

words.note: Like a choripán but with "morcilla", blood sausage. Asado and street-food classic.

example.es: Pedime un morcipán con chimichurri, porfa.
example.en: Order me a blood sausage sandwich with chimichurri, please.

words.note: "Ají" is often a hotter pepper. "Morrón rojo", "morrón verde".

example.es: Cortá el morrón en tiras para la pizza.
example.en: Cut the bell pepper into strips for the pizza.

words.note: Short for "muzzarella": the plain mozzarella pizza every pizzeria sells by the slice.

example.es: Pedimos una grande de muzza y dos porrones.
example.en: We ordered a large cheese pizza and two beers.

packs.name: Essentials VIII
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials VIII
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: The Andean word Argentines use; "aguacate" sounds Mexican or Spanish.

example.es: Me hice una tostada con palta y huevo.
example.en: I made myself avocado toast with egg.

words.note: The Christmas sweet bread with dried fruit, a must at Argentine Christmas.

example.es: Para Navidad nunca falta el pan dulce en la mesa.
example.en: At Christmas there's always sweet bread on the table.

words.note: Soft sandwich bread from the supermarket, as opposed to bakery bread.

example.es: Comprá pan lactal para hacer tostados.
example.en: Buy sliced bread to make toasted sandwiches.

words.note: A hot dog, sold everywhere with lots of sauces and "papas pay" on top.

example.es: Me comí dos panchos con papitas en la cancha.
example.en: I ate two hot dogs with chips at the stadium.

words.note: Both the grill itself and a restaurant specializing in grilled meat. "Vamos a una parrilla".

example.es: Hay una parrilla buenísima a dos cuadras de casa.
example.en: There's a great steakhouse two blocks from home.

packs.name: Essentials IX
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials IX
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Lattice tart filled with quince or sweet potato jam, perfect with mate.

example.es: Mi vieja hizo pastafrola para la merienda.
example.en: My mom made a jam tart for the afternoon snack.

words.note: A platter of cheese, salami, olives and bread shared before dinner or with drinks.

example.es: Armamos una picada con salame y queso para la previa.
example.en: We made a snack plate with salami and cheese for before the party.

words.note: The Buenos Aires word for popcorn. "Pororó" is used up north.

example.es: Compramos pochoclo antes de entrar al cine.
example.en: We bought popcorn before going into the movie.

words.note: A thick slice of provolone cheese grilled until melty, often with oregano. A classic asado starter.

example.es: Poné la provoleta en la parrilla mientras esperamos la carne.
example.en: Put the provolone on the grill while we wait for the meat.

packs.name: Essentials X
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials X
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: The everyday spoken form of "sándwich". "Sanguchito de miga" is a thin crustless sandwich.

example.es: Me hago un sanguche de jamón y queso y salgo.
example.en: I'll make a ham and cheese sandwich and head out.

words.note: The drinking straw. In Spain it's "pajita"; in Argentina you'd say "sorbete" or "pajita".

example.es: ¿Me das un sorbete para la gaseosa?
example.en: Can I have a straw for my soda?

words.note: A chicken milanesa. "Suprema a la napolitana" comes with ham, cheese and tomato sauce.

example.es: Para mí una suprema con puré, por favor.
example.en: A breaded chicken breast with mashed potatoes for me, please.

words.note: The round discs of dough for empanadas or tartas, bought ready-made at the supermarket.

example.es: Comprá tapas de empanada, que hoy cocino yo.
example.en: Buy empanada wrappers, I'm cooking tonight.

words.note: Usually savory: tarta de jamón y queso, de verdura, de choclo. A weeknight staple in every Argentine home.

example.es: Hoy cenamos tarta de jamón y queso con ensalada.
example.en: Tonight we're having ham and cheese pie with salad.

packs.name: Essentials XI
packs.title: Food & drink · Essentials XI
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: A grilled ham and cheese sandwich on sliced bread, the café classic with a coffee.

example.es: Un café con leche y un tostado de jamón y queso, por favor.
example.en: A latte and a toasted ham and cheese, please.

words.note: The tomato sauce for pasta, often slow-cooked with meat. Sunday "fideos con tuco" is a family ritual.

example.es: Los domingos mi vieja hace ñoquis con tuco.
example.en: On Sundays my mom makes gnocchi with tomato sauce.

words.note: A popular asado cut from the flank, juicy and with a layer of fat.

example.es: El vacío salió tiernísimo, ¿cuánto lo tuviste?
example.en: The meat came out very tender, how long did you cook it?

words.note: Short for "yerba mate", the dried leaves for mate. "Se lavó la yerba": the mate has lost its flavor.

example.es: Se terminó la yerba, bajá al chino a comprar.
example.en: We're out of mate leaves, go buy some at the store.

words.note: A small, round green squash, classic in Argentine cooking: stuffed, in tartas or in omelettes.

example.es: Hice zapallitos rellenos con carne y queso.
example.en: I made stuffed round zucchinis with meat and cheese.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Food & drink · Everyday
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Everyday veggie: roasted, in purée or in soups. "Zapallo" alone means pumpkin or squash.

example.es: Hacé un puré de zapallo anco para la cena.
example.en: Make mashed pumpkin for dinner.

words.note: Said of a steak or burger with fried eggs on top. A classic bodegón order: "bife a caballo".

example.es: Pedí un bife a caballo con papas fritas.
example.en: I ordered a steak with a fried egg on top and fries.

words.note: Very fine sugar for dusting cakes and "medialunas".

example.es: Espolvoreale azúcar impalpable al bizcochuelo antes de servir.
example.en: Put powdered sugar on the sponge cake before serving.

words.note: Small flaky crackers, often "de grasa", eaten with mate. Not a cake as in Spain.

example.es: Traé unos bizcochos de grasa para el mate.
example.en: Bring some crackers for the mate.

words.note: Loaf cake with candied fruit, sold at every bakery. A plain "budín" is any loaf cake.

example.es: Con el mate comimos un budín inglés.
example.en: We had fruitcake with our mate.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Food & drink · Going deeper I
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Finger food and drinks at an event or before a meal, like a small cocktail reception.

example.es: Después del acto hay un copetín en el salón.
example.en: After the ceremony there are drinks and snacks in the hall.

words.note: A horn-shaped pastry sold at bakeries, like a small croissant.

example.es: Traje cuernitos de la panadería para el mate.
example.en: I brought croissant rolls from the bakery for the mate.

words.note: A thin, flavorful cut from the diaphragm, a favorite at the parrilla.

example.es: Para mí, una entraña jugosa con papas fritas.
example.en: For me, a juicy skirt steak with fries.

words.note: Thin chickpea-flour bread from Genoa, eaten on top of a slice of pizza in Buenos Aires pizzerias.

example.es: Pedimos una grande de muzza con fainá.
example.en: We ordered a large mozzarella pizza with chickpea flatbread.

words.note: A long loaf of white bread. "¡La flauta!" is an old-fashioned exclamation of surprise.

example.es: Comprá una flauta en la panadería de la esquina.
example.en: Buy a baguette at the bakery on the corner.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Food & drink · Going deeper II
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Thin crunchy breadsticks, from Italian grissini.

example.es: Trajeron grisines con la picada.
example.en: They brought breadsticks with the snack plate.

words.note: Said in English. A favorite at every Argentine bakery.

example.es: De postre hay lemon pie.
example.en: There's lemon meringue pie for dessert.

words.note: Short-order food cooked on the spot: milanesa, omelette, fries. Menus say "minutas".

example.es: En ese bar hacen minutas baratas al mediodía.
example.en: That bar makes cheap quick dishes at lunch.

words.note: Casual word for food, from "morfar".

example.es: ¿Qué hay de morfi esta noche?
example.en: What food is there tonight?

words.note: Short for "napolitana": pizza with tomato slices, garlic and mozzarella.

example.es: Una media muzza y media napo, por favor.
example.en: Half cheese and half Neapolitan, please.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Food & drink · Going deeper III
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: A soft, slightly sweet roll, and the ham-and-cheese sandwich made with it.

example.es: Me pedí un pebete de jamón y queso.
example.en: I ordered a ham and cheese sandwich on a soft roll.

words.note: Full after eating. Casual, often with a pat on the belly.

example.es: Después del asado quedé pipón.
example.en: After the barbecue I was very full.

words.note: A milanesa topped like a pizza: tomato sauce, ham and mozzarella. Same as "milanesa a la napolitana".

example.es: Pedí una pizzanesa con papas fritas para compartir.
example.en: I ordered a pizza-topped schnitzel with fries to share.

words.note: A pre-baked dough with sauce sold in bakeries, ready for toppings at home.

example.es: Compré dos prepizzas y les pongo muzza.
example.en: I bought two pizza bases and I'll add mozzarella.

words.note: Always plural. A classic starter in porteño bodegones and a Mar del Plata beach favorite, usually with lemon.

example.es: Pidamos unas rabas para picar mientras esperamos.
example.en: Let's order some fried calamari to snack on while we wait.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Food & drink · Rare gems
packs.about: What Argentines eat and drink, and what they call it.

words.note: Sponge biscuits, usually plural "vainillas". Used in desserts or dunked in mate cocido.

example.es: Mojá las vainillas en café para el postre.
example.en: Dip the sponge cookies in coffee for the dessert.

words.note: A long "factura" with quince paste or custard. Legend says anarchist bakers named pastries to mock the police.

example.es: Comprá una docena de facturas: medialunas y vigilantes.
example.en: Buy a dozen pastries: croissants and jam pastries.

words.note: Hearty stew of tripe, beans and chorizo from Italian "busecca". Winter bodegón food.

example.es: En invierno mi abuelo hacía buseca los domingos.
example.en: In winter my grandpa made beef stomach stew on Sundays.

words.note: Aromatic herb from Córdoba's hills, added to mate or tea.

example.es: Le pongo una ramita de peperina al mate.
example.en: I add a little mountain mint to my mate.

words.note: A cantina-style creamy tomato sauce, usually on sorrentinos or ñoquis. Recipes vary by restaurant.

example.es: Pedí sorrentinos con salsa scarparo, están buenísimos acá.
example.en: Order the sorrentinos with scarparo sauce, they're great here.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: City & getting around · Essentials I
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: The usual word on Argentine beaches; "medusa" sounds bookish. Summer news warns about them.

example.es: No te metas al agua, que hay aguavivas.
example.en: Don't go in the water, there are jellyfish.

words.note: The neighborhood grocery; the owner is the "almacenero". Now often a Chinese-run "súper".

example.es: Voy al almacén de la esquina a comprar fiambre.
example.en: I'm going to the corner store to get cold cuts.

words.note: The strip beside a road or highway. "Irse a la banquina": to veer off the road.

example.es: Paramos en la banquina porque se pinchó una goma.
example.en: We stopped on the side of the road because we got a flat tire.

words.note: The lifeguard at the beach or pool, always with a whistle.

example.es: El bañero nos hizo salir porque había bandera roja.
example.en: The lifeguard made us get out because of the red flag.

words.note: The trunk of a car. "Maletero" and "cajuela" are other countries' words.

example.es: Poné las valijas en el baúl.
example.en: Put the suitcases in the trunk.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: City & getting around · Essentials II
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: Slang for a city bus; also "colectivo". Everyone says it.

example.es: Me tomo el bondi en la esquina y llego en diez.
example.en: I take the bus on the corner and get there in ten.

words.note: Found in plazas across Buenos Aires. Grab the "sortija" ring to win a free ride.

example.es: Llevamos a los nenes a la calesita de la plaza.
example.en: We took the kids to the merry-go-round in the plaza.

words.note: How people refer to the city proper, as opposed to "Provincia". "Vivo en Capital".

example.es: Vivo en Provincia pero trabajo en Capital.
example.en: I live in the province but work in the city.

words.note: "El chino" is the neighborhood grocery store, usually run by a Chinese family.

example.es: Bajo al chino a comprar pan y leche.
example.en: I'm going down to the corner store for bread and milk.

words.note: The city bus. Also "bondi" in slang.

example.es: Tomá el colectivo 60 hasta Constitución.
example.en: Take the 60 bus to Constitución.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: City & getting around · Essentials III
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: The edge of the sidewalk. Also a shoelace.

example.es: Estacioná pegado al cordón, que pasan los colectivos.
example.en: Park close to the edge of the sidewalk, buses pass here.

words.note: The length of one block, about 100 m, used to give distances: "a tres cuadras".

example.es: La farmacia está a dos cuadras, sobre la avenida.
example.en: The pharmacy is two blocks away, on the avenue.

words.note: A car or bike tire. In plural, slang for breasts.

example.es: Pinché una goma en la ruta.
example.en: I got a flat tire on the highway.

words.note: Small shop that fixes flat tires, found on every avenue and highway.

example.es: Pinché, ¿sabés si hay una gomería cerca?
example.en: I got a flat, do you know if there's a tire shop nearby?

words.note: "La gorra" is the police. "Ser gorra" is to be a snitch or buzzkill.

example.es: Guardá eso que viene la gorra.
example.en: Put that away, the cops are coming.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: City & getting around · Essentials IV
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: Tiny shops on every block selling candy, drinks, cigarettes and phone credit. Also spelled "kiosko".

example.es: Bajo al kiosco a comprar unos caramelos.
example.en: I'm going down to the kiosk for some candy.

words.note: Literally donkey's back.

example.es: Frená que hay un lomo de burro.
example.en: Slow down, there's a speed bump.

words.note: Mostly a long-distance coach; city buses are "colectivos" or "bondis".

example.es: Me tomo el micro a Mar del Plata a las once.
example.en: I'm catching the bus to Mar del Plata at eleven.

words.note: A thief who robs from a moving motorbike, a big fear in Buenos Aires streets.

example.es: Un motochorro le arrancó el celular de la mano.
example.en: A motorbike thief grabbed the phone out of her hand.

words.note: The normal word for a waiter in Argentina. Call him with "¡Mozo!" or a raised hand.

example.es: Mozo, ¿nos trae la cuenta, por favor?
example.en: Waiter, could you bring us the check, please?

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: City & getting around · Essentials V
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: Fuel for the car. "Cargar nafta" is to fill up.

example.es: Tengo que cargar nafta antes de salir a la ruta.
example.en: I have to get gas before the trip.

words.note: The car's license plate or number; also the yearly car tax.

example.es: ¿Anotaste la patente del auto que te chocó?
example.en: Did you write down the plate of the car that hit you?

words.note: In Argentina a driver's license is just "el registro". "Sacar el registro" = to get your license.

example.es: Me paró la policía y no tenía el registro encima.
example.en: The police stopped me and I didn't have my license on me.

words.note: A car with a driver that you book by phone or at an agency, with a fixed price. Plural: remises. The driver is a "remisero".

example.es: Pedí un remís para ir a Ezeiza a las seis.
example.en: I booked a taxi to go to Ezeiza airport at six.

words.note: A shop selling ready-made food to take home: roast chicken, empanadas, milanesas, tartas. A lifesaver on weeknights.

example.es: Compramos un pollo y papas en la rotisería de la esquina.
example.en: We bought a chicken and fries at the takeout shop on the corner.

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: City & getting around · Essentials VI
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: The rechargeable card for bus, subte and train. "Cargar la SUBE": to top it up.

example.es: No tengo saldo en la SUBE, ¿me prestás la tuya?
example.en: I have no credit on my transit card, can you lend me yours?

words.note: Short for subterráneo. Buenos Aires's metro, the oldest in Latin America. Lines are named by letter: la A, la B...

example.es: Tomate el subte en la línea D hasta Plaza Italia.
example.en: Take the subway on line D to Plaza Italia.

words.note: A doctor's or official appointment. "Sacar turno" = to book an appointment.

example.es: Tengo que sacar turno con el dentista.
example.en: I need to book an appointment with the dentist.

words.note: The Argentine word for "acera". "Cruzar a la vereda de enfrente": cross to the other side.

example.es: Caminá por la vereda, que la calle está llena de autos.
example.en: Walk on the sidewalk, the street is full of cars.

words.note: "La yuta" = the police, street slang. Not polite, not something to say to an officer.

example.es: Cayó la yuta y se terminó la fiesta.
example.en: The cops showed up and the party was over.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: City & getting around · Going deeper I
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: Bike paths, very common in Buenos Aires since the 2010s. Also "ciclovía".

example.es: Voy al laburo en bici por la bicisenda.
example.en: I bike to work on the bike lane.

words.note: Used in "vuelos de cabotaje": flights within Argentina.

example.es: Los vuelos de cabotaje salen de Aeroparque.
example.en: Domestic flights leave from Aeroparque.

words.note: The small bin in an office or on the street. At home, "tacho" is more common.

example.es: Tirá el papel en el cesto de basura de la esquina.
example.en: Throw the paper in the trash can on the corner.

words.note: The supermarket cart; the small one you pull home is a "changuito". In the northwest, "chango" means kid.

example.es: Agarrá un chango que vamos a comprar un montón.
example.en: Grab a shopping cart, we're buying a lot.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: City & getting around · Going deeper II
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: A minibus doing fixed routes between the suburbs and downtown, faster than the bondi.

example.es: Me tomo la combi a las siete para llegar al centro.
example.en: I catch the shuttle at seven to get downtown.

words.note: Driving against traffic on a one-way street: "ir de contramano". Figuratively, against the tide.

example.es: Casi chocamos, el tipo venía de contramano.
example.en: We nearly crashed, the guy was going the wrong way.

words.note: A short, narrow street, sometimes a dead end. Quieter than the avenues.

example.es: Vivo en una cortada muy tranquila de Palermo.
example.en: I live on a very quiet little side street in Palermo.

words.note: A private gated neighborhood in the suburbs, with security, lawns and often a golf course. Also "barrio cerrado".

example.es: Se mudaron a un country en Pilar y no los vemos más.
example.en: They moved to a gated community in Pilar and we never see them.

words.note: Used at the gomería, the tire shop. "Goma" is also common.

example.es: Se me pinchó una cubierta en la ruta.
example.en: I got a flat tire on the highway.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: City & getting around · Going deeper III
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: The person who sells papers at a kiosk, or delivers them.

example.es: El diariero de la esquina me guarda la revista.
example.en: The newspaper seller on the corner saves the magazine for me.

words.note: Everything outside Buenos Aires and its suburbs. Porteños say it a lot; provincials may find it snobby.

example.es: Mi familia es del interior, de un pueblo de Santa Fe.
example.en: My family is from outside Buenos Aires, from a town in Santa Fe.

words.note: Street slang for a gun. Car lovers call cars "fierros", and "meterle fierro" is to floor it.

example.es: El chorro tenía un fierro y nadie se movió.
example.en: The thief had a gun and nobody moved.

words.note: A ticket from a speed or red-light camera, mailed to you later.

example.es: Me llegó una fotomulta por pasar en rojo.
example.en: I got a camera fine for going through a red light.

words.note: In Argentina, the truck that tows badly parked or broken-down cars.

example.es: Estacioné mal y me llevó el auto el guinche.
example.en: I parked badly and the tow truck took my car.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: City & getting around · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: The highway ringing the city, the border between Capital and the conurbano.

example.es: A esta hora la General Paz está totalmente trabada.
example.en: At this time the ring road is completely full of traffic.

words.note: Also just "el giro". "Poner el giro" is to signal.

example.es: Poné la luz de giro antes de doblar.
example.en: Put your turn signal on before you turn.

words.note: The busy business center of Buenos Aires, full of offices, banks and street money changers.

example.es: Trabajo en el microcentro y almuerzo siempre al paso.
example.en: I work downtown and always eat lunch on the go.

words.note: A stand or joint selling "panchos", hot dogs. Common near stations.

example.es: Comimos en la panchería de la estación.
example.en: We ate at the hot dog stand by the station.

words.note: A roadside stop, or a beach club with loungers and a bar on the coast.

example.es: Alquilamos una sombrilla en el parador de la playa.
example.en: We rented an umbrella at the beach club.

packs.name: Going deeper V
packs.title: City & getting around · Going deeper V
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: A car bumper. A fender-bender is "un toque en el paragolpes".

example.es: Me rayaron el paragolpes estacionando.
example.en: Someone scratched my bumper while parking.

words.note: A district of Buenos Aires province, like La Matanza or Tigre. Also means match or party.

example.es: Vivo en el partido de San Isidro.
example.en: I live in San Isidro county.

words.note: The attendant at a gas station or parking lot. In Argentina they pump your gas.

example.es: El playero me limpió el parabrisas.
example.en: The gas station attendant cleaned my windshield.

words.note: A small shop selling a bit of everything: snacks, school supplies, gifts.

example.es: Comprá pilas en el polirubro de la esquina.
example.en: Buy batteries at the corner shop.

words.note: He brings glass soda siphons to your door every week. A porteño tradition that still survives in many neighborhoods.

example.es: Bajá que llegó el sodero con los sifones.
example.en: Go downstairs, the soda man is here with the soda bottles.

packs.name: Going deeper VI
packs.title: City & getting around · Going deeper VI
packs.about: Buses, the subte, shops and the street.

words.note: On the calesita, kids try to grab the ring hanging above them to win a free ride. Also an old gaucho horseback game.

example.es: Mi hijo sacó la sortija y ganó otra vuelta en la calesita.
example.en: My son grabbed the ring and won another ride on the merry-go-round.

words.note: The Argentine word for a bulldozer. A person who's unstoppable is "una topadora".

example.es: Pasó la topadora y tiró abajo la casa vieja.
example.en: The bulldozer came and knocked down the old house.

words.note: Informal settlements in and around Buenos Aires. Usually just "la villa". The official term is "barrio popular".

example.es: Creció en una villa miseria y hoy es médico.
example.en: He grew up in a slum and today he's a doctor.

words.note: The ticket inspector on trains and, in the past, on buses.

example.es: El guarda del tren me pidió el boleto.
example.en: The train conductor asked for my ticket.

words.note: The diagonal corner of buildings at intersections, typical of Buenos Aires. Often where shop doors sit.

example.es: Nos encontramos en la ochava, frente a la farmacia.
example.en: Let's meet at the corner, across from the pharmacy.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials I
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Argentine word for a stapler; elsewhere "grapadora". The staples are "ganchitos".

example.es: ¿Me pasás la abrochadora que está en tu escritorio?
example.en: Can you pass me the stapler on your desk?

words.note: Used to count rooms in listings: "un dos ambientes" is a one-bedroom apartment with a living room.

example.es: Alquilo un dos ambientes en Palermo.
example.en: I rent a one-bedroom apartment in Palermo.

words.note: The Argentine word; "arete" or "pendiente" elsewhere. Also any ring or hoop.

example.es: Qué lindos aros, ¿dónde los compraste?
example.en: What pretty earrings, where did you buy them?

words.note: The kitchen or bathroom sink basin. Also "pileta de la cocina".

example.es: Dejá los platos en la bacha, después los lavo.
example.en: Leave the dishes in the sink, I'll wash them later.

words.note: The Argentine word for a bathtub. Also an old open-top bus rented for groups.

example.es: Llené la bañadera y me quedé una hora adentro.
example.en: I filled the bathtub and stayed in for an hour.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials II
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: From László Bíró, who developed the pen in Argentina. The everyday word for a pen.

example.es: ¿Me prestás una birome para firmar?
example.en: Can you lend me a pen to sign?

words.note: The Argentine name for a sleeping bag, needed for camping trips.

example.es: Llevá la bolsa de dormir que a la noche hace frío.
example.en: Bring your sleeping bag, it gets cold at night.

words.note: Women's underwear. "Bombachas de campo" are gaucho baggy pants.

example.es: Compré bombachas nuevas en el shopping.
example.en: I bought new panties at the mall.

words.note: The metal straw with a filter used to drink mate. Never stir it; the cebador will get upset.

example.es: No muevas la bombilla, que se tapa.
example.en: Don't move the straw, it'll clog.

words.note: From French "bordeaux". The color, used for clothes and team shirts.

example.es: Me puse la campera bordó.
example.en: I put on my dark red jacket.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials III
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: The peg for hanging clothes. "Broches" are also staples.

example.es: Pasame los broches, que cuelgo la ropa.
example.en: Pass me the clothespins, I'll hang the laundry.

words.note: Any sweatshirt or hoodie. "Buzo de egresados": the class hoodie seniors get.

example.es: Ponete un buzo que está refrescando.
example.en: Put on a sweatshirt, it's getting chilly.

words.note: The gas heater that warms water as it runs. Tango "Cambalache" mentions the Bible next to the calefón.

example.es: Se apagó el calefón y me bañé con agua fría.
example.en: The water heater stopped working and I showered in cold water.

words.note: Tight leggings for the gym or everyday wear. Usually singular.

example.es: Me puse la calza para ir al gimnasio.
example.en: I put on my leggings to go to the gym.

words.note: Any casual jacket or coat. "Campera de jean", "campera de cuero".

example.es: Llevate la campera, que a la noche refresca.
example.en: Take your jacket, it gets chilly at night.
