packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials IV
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: The everyday word for a tap in Argentina. Spain says "grifo".

example.es: Cerrá bien la canilla que gotea toda la noche.
example.en: Turn the faucet off tight, it drips all night.

words.note: The shirt with a collar and buttons. Very common word.

example.es: Para el laburo me pongo chomba y jean.
example.en: For work I wear a polo shirt and jeans.

words.note: A parking spot or garage, in a house or rented monthly in a building.

example.es: Alquilo una cochera a una cuadra de casa.
example.en: I rent a parking spot a block from home.

words.note: The everyday word in Argentina. Spain says "sujetador".

example.es: Me compré un corpiño nuevo en el shopping.
example.en: I bought a new bra at the mall.

words.note: A dog's bed or house. "¡A la cucha!" means go to bed, even jokingly to people.

example.es: El perro duerme en la cucha del patio.
example.en: The dog sleeps in the doghouse in the yard.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials V
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Porteños mostly live in "deptos". Spain says "piso".

example.es: Alquilamos un departamento de dos ambientes en Almagro.
example.en: We rent a one-bedroom apartment in Almagro.

words.note: In Argentina an estufa is a room heater, not a stove. The kitchen stove is the cocina.

example.es: Prendé la estufa, que me estoy congelando.
example.en: Turn on the heater, I'm freezing.

words.note: Bottled gas used for cooking where there's no gas line.

example.es: Se acabó la garrafa y no podemos cocinar.
example.en: The gas canister ran out and we can't cook.

words.note: Nevera or refrigerador elsewhere.

example.es: Dejé la birra en la heladera.
example.en: I left the beer in the fridge.

words.note: Track pants or sweatpants, pronounced "yo-guin". Also "pantalón de jogging".

example.es: Los domingos no me saco el jogging en todo el día.
example.en: On Sundays I don't take off my sweatpants all day.

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials VI
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Lavadora elsewhere.

example.es: Poné la ropa en el lavarropas antes de irte.
example.en: Put the clothes in the washing machine before you go.

words.note: Borrowed from English. Also living-comedor.

example.es: Los chicos están mirando tele en el living.
example.en: The kids are watching TV in the living room.

words.note: Any swimsuit or trunks. "Malla enteriza" is a one-piece.

example.es: No te olvides la malla, que hay pileta.
example.en: Don't forget your swimsuit, there's a pool.

words.note: Biberón or tetero elsewhere.

example.es: Calentá la mamadera que el bebé tiene hambre.
example.en: Warm up the bottle, the baby is hungry.

words.note: The bedside table, literally "light table" because the lamp sits on it.

example.es: Dejé el celular cargando en la mesa de luz.
example.en: I left my phone charging on the nightstand.

packs.name: Essentials VII
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials VII
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: The kitchen countertop. Elsewhere it means an allowance, but in Argentina think counter first.

example.es: Dejá los platos sucios en la mesada, después los lavo.
example.en: Leave the dirty dishes on the counter, I'll wash them later.

words.note: A one-room apartment, the classic first rental in Buenos Aires.

example.es: Alquilo un monoambiente chiquito en Palermo.
example.en: I rent a tiny studio in Palermo.

words.note: A sleeveless top, for summer or the gym.

example.es: Con este calor me pongo una musculosa y listo.
example.en: In this heat I'll put on a tank top and that's it.

words.note: Rubber sandals for the beach or the house. Usually plural.

example.es: Ponete las ojotas, que la arena quema.
example.en: Put on your flip-flops, the sand is burning.

words.note: The kettle for mate water. "Poner la pava" is to put the water on.

example.es: Poné la pava que hacemos unos mates.
example.en: Put the kettle on and we'll have some mate.

packs.name: Essentials VIII
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials VIII
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Everyday word for a bedroom, especially your own room at home.

example.es: Andá a ordenar tu pieza antes de salir.
example.en: Go tidy your room before you go out.

words.note: The normal word for a pool; "piscina" sounds foreign. Also a sink.

example.es: Los chicos se pasan el día en la pileta.
example.en: The kids spend all day in the pool.

words.note: From French. The built-in wardrobe in a bedroom. Pronounced "pla-CAR".

example.es: Tu campera está colgada en el placard.
example.en: Your jacket is hanging in the closet.

words.note: A roofed outdoor space with a grill, used for asados with friends. Many buildings and clubs have one.

example.es: El sábado hacemos un asado en el quincho del edificio.
example.en: On Saturday we're having a barbecue in the building's barbecue area.

words.note: The standard word in Argentina. You'll rarely hear "camiseta", which means a sports jersey or undershirt.

example.es: Me compré una remera de los Redondos en la feria.
example.en: I bought a Redondos T-shirt at the street market.

packs.name: Essentials IX
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials IX
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: The cloth you dry dishes with. Every Argentine kitchen has one hanging from the oven door.

example.es: Pasame el repasador que seco los platos.
example.en: Hand me the dish towel and I'll dry the plates.

words.note: From "riñón", kidney, since it sits on your waist. Common for festivals, travel and crowded places.

example.es: Guardá el celu en la riñonera, que en el recital roban.
example.en: Keep your phone in the waist bag, people steal at concerts.

words.note: In Argentina "tacos" are high heels or shoe heels, not Mexican food. "Zapatos de taco" = heels.

example.es: No voy a bailar toda la noche con estos tacos.
example.en: I'm not dancing all night in these heels.

words.note: Originally a brand name. Used for takeout ice cream containers, packaging and school projects.

example.es: El helado viene en un pote de telgopor.
example.en: The ice cream comes in a styrofoam tub.

packs.name: Essentials X
packs.title: Home & clothes · Essentials X
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: The flask of hot water for mate, carried everywhere under the arm.

example.es: Siempre ando con el termo y el mate en la mochila.
example.en: I always carry the thermos and mate in my backpack.

words.note: A tank that stores hot water for the house, unlike the instant "calefón".

example.es: Hay que cambiar el termotanque, ya no calienta nada.
example.en: We need to replace the water heater, it doesn't heat at all anymore.

words.note: A big bath or beach towel, as opposed to a small "toalla".

example.es: Llevá un toallón para tirarte en la arena.
example.en: Bring a big towel to lie on the sand.

words.note: The usual word in Argentina; "maleta" sounds foreign. "Armar la valija" = to pack.

example.es: Todavía no armé la valija y el vuelo sale a las ocho.
example.en: I still haven't packed my suitcase and the flight leaves at eight.

words.note: The small lamp on your nightstand. In some countries it means the nightstand itself.

example.es: Apagá el velador, que quiero dormir.
example.en: Turn off the bedside lamp, I want to sleep.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Home & clothes · Everyday
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: The everyday word for sneakers or trainers, not slippers as in Spain.

example.es: Me compré unas zapatillas nuevas para correr.
example.en: I bought some new sneakers for running.

words.note: A quilt or comforter on the bed. In winter you add a "frazada", a blanket, too.

example.es: Sacá el acolchado, que ya hace frío.
example.en: Get the duvet out, it's cold now.

words.note: The everyday Argentine name for a safety pin.

example.es: Se me rompió el cierre, ¿tenés un alfiler de gancho?
example.en: My zipper broke, do you have a safety pin?

words.note: In Argentina "alicate" is the small clipper for nails or cuticles, not just pliers.

example.es: ¿Viste el alicate? Me tengo que cortar las uñas.
example.en: Have you seen the nail clippers? I need to cut my nails.

words.note: Small pad for jotting things down. Common in offices and kitchens.

example.es: Anotalo en el anotador que está al lado del teléfono.
example.en: Write it on the notepad next to the phone.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Home & clothes · Going deeper I
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Swimming or safety goggles. Usually plural.

example.es: Llevá las antiparras que el cloro te irrita los ojos.
example.en: Bring your goggles, the chlorine irritates your eyes.

words.note: Lace-up ankle boots, military or fashion style. Usually plural.

example.es: Me compré unos borcegos negros para el invierno.
example.en: I bought some black combat boots for winter.

words.note: Garden tool to trim grass edges. Weekend noise in the suburbs.

example.es: El vecino está con la bordeadora desde las ocho.
example.en: The neighbor has been using the grass trimmer since eight.

words.note: A bed raised on built-in drawers. A pull-out second bed is a "cama nido"; bunk beds are "cucheta".

example.es: Compramos una cama marinera para ganar lugar en la pieza.
example.en: We bought a bed with drawers to save space in the bedroom.

words.note: The basket where dirty clothes go. Also any big basket.

example.es: Tirá la remera sucia en el canasto, por favor.
example.en: Throw the dirty T-shirt in the laundry basket, please.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Home & clothes · Going deeper II
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: A toy or a cute gadget. "Estar como un chiche" means spotless and shiny.

example.es: El nene no suelta su chiche nuevo.
example.en: The little boy won't let go of his new toy.

words.note: "Pasto" is the Argentine word for grass or lawn.

example.es: El vecino prende la cortadora de pasto los domingos a las ocho.
example.en: The neighbor starts his lawnmower at eight on Sundays.

words.note: The stiff push broom used for patios and floors. Escoba is also used.

example.es: Pasá el escobillón por el patio, que está lleno de hojas.
example.en: Sweep the patio, it's full of leaves.

words.note: Usually just called "la flor". Literally the shower's flower.

example.es: Se tapó la flor de la ducha y sale poca agua.
example.en: The showerhead is clogged and barely any water comes out.

words.note: Kid's slingshot. Elsewhere tirachinas or resortera.

example.es: De chico rompía vidrios con la gomera.
example.en: As a kid I used to break windows with my slingshot.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Home & clothes · Going deeper III
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Playground swing. A hammock is a hamaca paraguaya.

example.es: Los chicos están en las hamacas de la plaza.
example.en: The kids are on the swings at the park.

words.note: Literally a Paraguayan swing.

example.es: Colgamos la hamaca paraguaya entre los dos árboles.
example.en: We hung the hammock between the two trees.

words.note: Kitchen blender for licuados and juices. Many people also say "licuadora".

example.es: Pasame la juguera que hago un licuado.
example.en: Hand me the blender and I'll make a smoothie.

words.note: In Argentina a drill bit is a "mecha". Also means a wick or a lock of hair.

example.es: Necesito una mecha más fina para este taladro.
example.en: I need a thinner bit for this drill.

words.note: A maid in a house or hotel. The masculine "mucamo" exists but is rare.

example.es: La mucama del hotel nos dejó toallas limpias.
example.en: The hotel maid left us clean towels.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: Home & clothes · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Swim fins, literally "frog's foot". Usually plural: "patas de rana".

example.es: Llevá las patas de rana para hacer snorkel.
example.en: Bring the flippers for snorkeling.

words.note: A "propiedad horizontal": a house or apartment reached through a hallway, often with a patio. Said "pe hache".

example.es: Vivimos en un PH con terraza propia.
example.en: We live in a house behind another house, with its own terrace.

words.note: Casual word for clothes, usually plural: "las pilchas". From gaucho speech.

example.es: Me compré pilchas nuevas para el casamiento.
example.en: I bought new clothes for the wedding.

words.note: A light raincoat, from the aviators' coats. Not a pilot in this sense.

example.es: Está por llover, llevate el piloto.
example.en: It's about to rain, take your raincoat.

words.note: A soft cotton bucket hat, a summer classic for kids and fishermen.

example.es: Ponele el piluso al nene que pega fuerte el sol.
example.en: Put the bucket hat on the kid, the sun is strong.

packs.name: Going deeper V
packs.title: Home & clothes · Going deeper V
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Shallow or flat, mainly "plato playo", a dinner plate, versus "plato hondo".

example.es: Poné platos playos para la carne.
example.en: Set out dinner plates for the meat.

words.note: A turtleneck sweater or top. In Chile it means T-shirt, so watch out.

example.es: Hace frío, ponete la polera negra.
example.en: It's cold, put on the black turtleneck.

words.note: "Pollera" is the Argentine word for skirt; "tubo" is the tight, straight cut.

example.es: Para la entrevista me puse una pollera tubo.
example.en: I wore a pencil skirt for the interview.

words.note: The building door buzzer and speaker. "Tocá el portero" means ring the buzzer.

example.es: Tocá el portero, que te abro.
example.en: Ring the intercom and I'll let you in.

words.note: A knit sweater, from English "pullover". Also written "pullover".

example.es: Ponete un pulóver, que hace frío.
example.en: Put on a sweater, it's cold.

packs.name: Going deeper VI
packs.title: Home & clothes · Going deeper VI
packs.about: Things around the house and what you wear.

words.note: Real estate word for an apartment taking up half a floor of a building, a step up from a regular flat.

example.es: Se mudaron a un semipiso en Palermo con balcón.
example.en: They moved to a half-floor apartment in Palermo with a balcony.

words.note: From French, said "sutién". A bit old-fashioned; "corpiño" is more common today.

example.es: Se me rompió el soutien justo antes de salir.
example.en: My bra broke right before going out.

words.note: A long, elegant winter coat, mostly women's. Sounds a bit classic; "abrigo" also works.

example.es: Ponete el tapado, que afuera hace un frío terrible.
example.en: Put on your coat, it's freezing outside.

words.note: A mop with a long handle. Many people say trapo de piso.

example.es: Pasá el lampazo por la cocina, que está mojada.
example.en: Mop the kitchen, it's wet.

words.note: Childhood game played with five little stones or pieces. Mostly a nostalgia word now.

example.es: De chica jugaba a la payana en el patio.
example.en: As a girl I played jacks in the yard.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Body & looks · Essentials I
packs.about: Body parts and how people look.

words.note: Cheek of the face. "Cachetón" is chubby-cheeked; grandmas love to pinch them.

example.es: La abuela siempre le aprieta los cachetes al nene.
example.en: Grandma always pinches the kid's cheeks.

words.note: A good-looking guy or girl. Also the fried pastry.

example.es: El nuevo del gimnasio es un churro.
example.en: The new guy at the gym is really attractive.

words.note: Also a hair tie: "¿tenés una colita?". Childish word for butt too.

example.es: Hacete una colita que hace mucho calor.
example.en: Put your hair in a ponytail, it's really hot.

words.note: Argentines say "colorado" or "colorada" for a redhead. Also means red in the face.

example.es: La colorada de la foto es mi hermana.
example.en: The redhead in the photo is my sister.

words.note: Someone's appearance or style. "Tener buena facha" is to be good-looking; "¡qué facha!" can be ironic.

example.es: Ese chico tiene buena facha, ¿no?
example.en: That guy is good-looking, right?

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Body & looks · Essentials II
packs.about: Body parts and how people look.

words.note: Very common compliment for someone who looks sharp. Can also mean a bit of a show-off.

example.es: Estás re fachero con esa campera nueva.
example.en: You look really good in that new jacket.

words.note: Informal, from Italian. "Hacer la gamba" means to keep someone company or back them up.

example.es: Me duele la gamba de tanto caminar.
example.en: My leg hurts from walking so much.

words.note: Dark-haired or dark-skinned. Used neutrally and even as a nickname: "¿Qué hacés, morocho?"

example.es: Mi hermana es la morocha de rulos.
example.en: My sister is the dark-haired one with curls.

words.note: Bald, or a bald man. Common and friendly nickname: "el Pelado". "Pelada" is a bald head.

example.es: El pelado de anteojos es mi profe de historia.
example.en: The bald guy with glasses is my history teacher.

words.note: Everyday word for chin, literally "pear". "Mentón" sounds more formal.

example.es: Se hizo un corte en la pera afeitándose.
example.en: He cut his chin shaving.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Body & looks · Essentials III
packs.about: Body parts and how people look.

words.note: Short in height; also an affectionate nickname. The normal word, not "bajo".

example.es: Soy medio petiso para jugar al básquet.
example.en: I'm kind of short to play basketball.

words.note: Attractive, handsome. Warm and a bit old-fashioned but still very common. "Pintona" for women.

example.es: El hermano de Sofi es re pintón.
example.en: Sofi's brother is really good-looking.

words.note: A punch. "Se agarraron a piñas" means they got into a fistfight.

example.es: Se agarraron a piñas a la salida del boliche.
example.en: They started a fight outside the club.

words.note: Everyday, a bit childish-sounding word. Adults use it too, especially with kids or jokingly.

example.es: El nene se ríe cuando le hacés cosquillas en el pupo.
example.en: The little boy laughs when you tickle his belly button.

words.note: Curly hair. "Tener rulos" is to have curly hair; "ruludo" is curly-haired.

example.es: Me encantan tus rulos, ¿te los hacés o son naturales?
example.en: I love your curls, do you do them or are they natural?

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Body & looks · Going deeper I
packs.about: Body parts and how people look.

words.note: A salon blow-dry. Pronounced "brá-shin". "Hacerse el brushing" before a party.

example.es: Me hice el brushing para el casamiento.
example.en: I got a blow-dry for the wedding.

words.note: Near-sighted, can't see well without glasses. Informal and a bit teasing.

example.es: Soy re chicato, sin anteojos no veo el pizarrón.
example.en: I'm really short-sighted, without glasses I can't see the board.

words.note: Bow-legged, or crooked in general: "el cuadro está chueco". Fangio's nickname was "el Chueco".

example.es: Camina medio chueco desde que se lesionó.
example.en: He's walked a bit crooked since he got hurt.

words.note: Lighter streaks dyed into the hair. "Hacerse claritos" at the hairdresser.

example.es: Me hice claritos y quedé re rubia.
example.en: I got highlights and ended up really blonde.

words.note: The neck, especially the back of it. Informal. "Estar hasta el cogote" is to be up to your neck.

example.es: Dormí mal y me duele el cogote.
example.en: I slept badly and my neck hurts.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Body & looks · Going deeper II
packs.about: Body parts and how people look.

words.note: Said of someone physically attractive. "Está re fuerte" means he or she is really hot.

example.es: ¿Viste al nuevo del gimnasio? Está re fuerte.
example.en: Did you see the new guy at the gym? He's really attractive.

words.note: At the gym, "hacer fierros" is lifting weights.

example.es: Voy al gimnasio a hacer fierros tres veces por semana.
example.en: I go to the gym to lift weights three times a week.

words.note: An elastic band for tying hair. "¿Tenés una gomita?" is a constant question.

example.es: ¿Tenés una gomita para atarme el pelo?
example.en: Do you have a hair tie so I can tie my hair up?

words.note: A clip or bobby pin for the hair. Elsewhere it only means belt buckle.

example.es: Se me cayó la hebilla y tengo el pelo en la cara.
example.en: My hair clip fell and my hair is in my face.

words.note: Slang for a great body. "Tener un lomazo" is to be really fit.

example.es: Mirá el lomazo que tiene ese chabón.
example.en: Look at the great body that guy has.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Body & looks · Going deeper III
packs.about: Body parts and how people look.

words.note: Very tall and thin. From Italian. Also a nickname: "el Lungo".

example.es: Mi primo es un lungo de dos metros.
example.en: My cousin is very tall and thin, two meters tall.

words.note: Child talk for a small hurt; adults use "nanas" for aches and pains of age.

example.es: Vení que te beso la nana y se te pasa.
example.en: Come here, I'll kiss where it hurts and it'll go away.

words.note: Casual for nose. "Con la ñata contra el vidrio" means watching from outside, left out.

example.es: Me pegaron un pelotazo en la ñata.
example.en: I got hit in the nose by a ball.

words.note: Child talk for pee: "hacer pichí". Adults use it jokingly.

example.es: Antes de salir, andá a hacer pichí.
example.en: Go pee before we leave.

words.note: The flat iron for straightening hair. "Pasarse la planchita" is to straighten it.

example.es: Me paso la planchita y salgo.
example.en: I'll straighten my hair and head out.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Body & looks · Rare gems
packs.about: Body parts and how people look.

words.note: Limping or lame. "Quedar rengo" after an injury. The usual word in Argentina instead of "cojo".

example.es: Me doblé el tobillo y estoy rengo.
example.en: I twisted my ankle and I'm limping.

words.note: A bun of hair on top or at the back of the head. "Hacerse un rodete".

example.es: Hacete un rodete que hace un calor bárbaro.
example.en: Put your hair in a bun, it's really hot.

words.note: Handsome in the face, often with a touch of irony: the pretty boy.

example.es: Ese carilindo se cree que todas se mueren por él.
example.en: That pretty boy thinks every girl is crazy about him.

words.note: A small beard on the chin only. From "chivo", goat.

example.es: Se afeitó todo y se dejó la chivita.
example.en: He shaved everything but kept the goatee.

words.note: Old slang for head, still heard in jokes: "¿Qué tenés en el marote?".

example.es: Ponete el gorro que se te congela el marote.
example.en: Put on your hat or your head will freeze.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Moods & feelings · Essentials I
packs.about: Being bored, tired, fed up or thrilled.

words.note: "Estar a mil": extremely busy or wound up. Informal.

example.es: Perdón que no te llamé, estoy a mil con la mudanza.
example.en: Sorry I didn't call, I'm very busy with the move.

words.note: A slump, sadness or letdown: "¡qué bajón!". "Estar de bajón": to feel down. Very common.

example.es: Qué bajón que se suspendió el recital.
example.en: What a shame that the concert got cancelled.

words.note: Anger or frustration: "me da bronca", it makes me mad. Very common everyday word.

example.es: Me da bronca que nadie avise cuando llega tarde.
example.en: It makes me angry when people don't tell you they'll be late.

words.note: To get angry: "no te calientes". "Estar caliente" can mean angry, but careful: it also means horny.

example.es: No te calentés, fue sin querer.
example.en: Don't get mad, it was an accident.

words.note: Used a lot for things and people that wear you out.

example.es: Viajar dos horas en el tren es muy cansador.
example.en: Riding the train for two hours is really tiring.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Moods & feelings · Essentials II
packs.about: Being bored, tired, fed up or thrilled.

words.note: Delighted, tickled pink: "está chocha con el nieto". Warm, a bit old-fashioned but common.

example.es: Mi abuela está chocha con el perrito nuevo.
example.en: My grandma is very happy with the new puppy.

words.note: Distracted or forgetful: "soy re colgado". "Me colgué": I forgot. Informal.

example.es: Hoy estoy re colgado, me olvidé las llaves otra vez.
example.en: I'm so distracted today, I forgot my keys again.

words.note: Exhausted, or in bad shape after a rough night.

example.es: Llegué detonado del laburo, me voy a dormir.
example.en: I got home very tired from work, I'm going to bed.

words.note: To get bored stiff. Informal, very common; "me embolé" after a dull movie.

example.es: Me embolé en la clase y me fui a la mitad.
example.en: I got bored in class and left halfway through.

words.note: Something boring. "¡Qué embole!" means what a drag.

example.es: La reunión fue un embole, dos horas de nada.
example.en: The meeting was really boring, two hours of nothing.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Moods & feelings · Essentials III
packs.about: Being bored, tired, fed up or thrilled.

words.note: Distracted, or into other things now: "ya está en otra". Informal.

example.es: Te hablo y no me escuchás, estás en otra.
example.en: I'm talking to you and you're not listening, your mind is somewhere else.

words.note: That lazy can't-be-bothered feeling. "Me da fiaca" means I can't be bothered.

example.es: Hoy tengo una fiaca bárbara, no quiero salir.
example.en: I'm feeling really lazy today, I don't want to go out.

words.note: Exhausted, or emotionally wrecked. Literally made into a ball.

example.es: Llegué hecho pelota del laburo.
example.en: I got home from work exhausted.

words.note: Bad luck, or a person who brings it. "Estar con mufa" is also to be in a bad mood. Very common in football talk.

example.es: No lo invites a la cancha, es un mufa.
example.en: Don't invite him to the game, he brings bad luck.

words.note: "Estar podrido de algo": sick and tired of it. Informal; literally rotten.

example.es: Estoy podrido de que me cancelen a último momento.
example.en: I'm sick of people cancelling at the last minute.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Moods & feelings · Everyday
packs.about: Being bored, tired, fed up or thrilled.

words.note: "Estar quemado": mentally fried from work or study. "Tengo la cabeza quemada". Informal.

example.es: Después de seis horas de reunión estoy re quemado.
example.en: After six hours of meetings I'm really tired.

words.note: To be unable to stop laughing, often at the wrong moment: "me tenté". Very Argentine.

example.es: En el velorio me tenté y tuve que salir.
example.en: At the wake I started laughing and had to leave.

words.note: Bitter, no fun: "no seas amargo". Used for someone who won't join in. Informal.

example.es: Dale, no seas amargo y vení a bailar.
example.en: Come on, don't be boring and come dance.

words.note: Grumpy, crabby: "hoy el jefe está cruzado". Informal.

example.es: Hoy mi viejo anda cruzado, mejor no le hables.
example.en: My dad is in a bad mood today, better not talk to him.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Moods & feelings · Going deeper I
packs.about: Being bored, tired, fed up or thrilled.

words.note: "Estar del tomate": to be nuts. Jokey, informal.

example.es: Querés cruzar la cordillera en bici, estás del tomate.
example.en: You want to cross the Andes by bike, you're crazy.

words.note: Excited and carried away: "estoy embalado con el proyecto". Informal.

example.es: Está embalado con la banda, ensaya todos los días.
example.en: He's very excited about the band, he practices every day.

words.note: To get tangled up overthinking something: "no te enrosques". Informal.

example.es: No te enrosques, seguro no te contestó porque estaba laburando.
example.en: Don't overthink it, he surely didn't reply because he was working.

words.note: To be crazy or overwhelmed: "estás de la cabeza". Also stressed out. Informal.

example.es: Con tres laburos, Pablo está de la cabeza.
example.en: With three jobs, Pablo is going crazy.

words.note: Utterly exhausted: "llegué fusilado". Informal; literally shot by firing squad.

example.es: Después del turno doble llegué fusilado a casa.
example.en: After the double shift I got home exhausted.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Moods & feelings · Going deeper II
packs.about: Being bored, tired, fed up or thrilled.

words.note: Overwhelmed and overthinking, or dazed from drugs. A "mambo" is a mental mess.

example.es: Estoy re mambeado con el laburo, no duermo.
example.en: I'm really stressed with work, I can't sleep.

words.note: "Tirar una pálida" is to bring everyone down with bad news or negativity.

example.es: No tires pálidas, que estamos de festejo.
example.en: Don't be negative, we're celebrating.

words.note: "Estar rayado": obsessed with something, or a bit crazy. Informal, youthful.

example.es: Está rayado con el gimnasio, va todos los días.
example.en: He's obsessed with the gym, he goes every day.

words.note: Beside oneself with rage, or wild: "estaba re sacado". Informal.

example.es: El vecino vino re sacado por el ruido.
example.en: The neighbor came over furious about the noise.

words.note: Like a frozen computer: stuck, blank. "Me quedé tildado": my mind went blank. Informal.

example.es: Me preguntó el nombre y me quedé tildado.
example.en: He asked my name and I just froze.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Moods & feelings · Rare gems
packs.about: Being bored, tired, fed up or thrilled.

words.note: "Estar tragado": totally smitten with someone. Informal.

example.es: Está re tragado con su compañera de facultad.
example.en: He's really in love with his classmate.

words.note: A passion or whim you can't let go of, like a hobby or dream. Tango-era, still used.

example.es: Su berretín es tener un auto antiguo.
example.en: His big dream is to own an old car.

words.note: "Estar camote de alguien": to be smitten. The vegetable is "batata" in Buenos Aires.

example.es: Está camote de la chica de la oficina.
example.en: He's really in love with the girl from the office.

words.note: A scare: "me pegué un julepe bárbaro". Rioplatense, a bit old-fashioned.

example.es: Me pegué un julepe cuando sonó el teléfono a las tres.
example.en: I got a real scare when the phone rang at three.

words.note: An intense crush or obsession: "tiene un metejón con la vecina". Lunfardo, still used.

example.es: Tiene un metejón con esa chica que no se le pasa.
example.en: He's in love with that girl and he can't forget her.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Essentials I
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: Argentines say agarrar, never coger, for take or grab: "agarrá el colectivo", "agarrá por Corrientes".

example.es: Agarrá la segunda a la derecha y ya llegaste.
example.en: Take the second right and you're there.

words.note: "¿Te animás?": are you up for it? Used constantly for daring or feeling up to something.

example.es: ¿Te animás a tirarte del trampolín?
example.en: Do you dare to jump off the diving board?

words.note: Start or head off: "¿arrancamos?", "arranqué el gimnasio". Much more common than empezar in speech.

example.es: ¿Arrancamos? Ya son las diez.
example.en: Shall we start? It's already ten.

words.note: "No lo banco": I can't stand him. Also to back someone: "yo te banco". "Bancátela": deal with it.

example.es: No lo banco más a mi jefe.
example.en: I can't put up with my boss anymore.

words.note: To insult, provoke or mess with someone. Also to make trouble.

example.es: Dejá de bardear a tu hermana.
example.en: Stop bothering your sister.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Essentials II
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: To fail someone on an exam: "me bocharon en química". Student slang.

example.es: Me bocharon en el final de matemática.
example.en: They failed me on the math final.

words.note: To waste time doing nothing useful. Also to mess with or fool someone.

example.es: Dejá de boludear con el celular y ayudame.
example.en: Stop wasting time on your phone and help me.

words.note: To tell on someone. Kids and adults both use it.

example.es: No me buchonees, porfa.
example.en: Don't tell on me, please.

words.note: To prepare and serve mate in rounds: "¿quién ceba?". Also to egg someone on.

example.es: ¿Cebás vos? A mí siempre me sale lavado.
example.en: Will you serve the mate? Mine always comes out weak.

words.note: To flirt with smooth talk, or to bluff. Lunfardo, used by everyone.

example.es: Estuvo toda la noche chamuyando a la chica de la barra.
example.en: He spent all night flirting with the girl at the bar.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Essentials III
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: Everyday verb for check or verify, preferred over "comprobar". Neutral.

example.es: Chequeá que la puerta quede cerrada antes de salir.
example.en: Check that the door is locked before you leave.

words.note: Informal, from "chorro", thief. Very common.

example.es: Me chorearon el celular en el subte.
example.en: They stole my phone on the subway.

words.note: To gossip or nose around. Also to browse: "chusmear el menú".

example.es: Estaba chusmeando tu Instagram y vi las fotos del viaje.
example.en: I was looking at your Instagram and saw the trip photos.

words.note: "Me clavó": stood me up. "Clavar el visto": leave on read. Also stick someone with a cost.

example.es: Me clavó una hora en el bar y nunca vino.
example.en: He left me waiting an hour at the bar and never came.

words.note: "Me copa" means I love it. "Coparse" means to get into something.

example.es: Me copa mucho esa banda, ¿vamos al recital?
example.en: I really like that band, do you want to go to the concert?

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Essentials IV
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: "Correte" means move over. "Correr la mesa" is to move the table.

example.es: Correte un poco que no entro en el sillón.
example.en: Move over a bit, I don't fit on the sofa.

words.note: To stop doing something annoying: "¡cortala!". Informal, common with kids and friends.

example.es: Cortala con el celular y ayudame a poner la mesa.
example.en: Stop it with the phone and help me set the table.

words.note: Used for exams: "desaprobé matemática". The opposite is "aprobar".

example.es: Desaprobé el parcial y lo tengo que recuperar.
example.en: I failed the exam and have to take it again.

words.note: To screw things up: "la embarré". Informal, not rude.

example.es: La embarré, le conté la sorpresa a Juan.
example.en: I messed up, I told Juan about the surprise.

words.note: To get into something: "me enganché con la serie". Also to join in. Informal.

example.es: Me enganché con la serie y la terminé en dos días.
example.en: I really got into the show and finished it in two days.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Essentials V
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: To imagine something that isn't true, or to be amazed. "Flasheaste" means you're imagining things.

example.es: Flasheaste, yo nunca dije eso.
example.en: You're imagining things, I never said that.

words.note: Slang for funcionar, used for machines and plans.

example.es: El wifi no funca, reinicialo.
example.en: The wifi isn't working, restart it.

words.note: From English. To stop answering someone without explanation.

example.es: Salimos dos veces y después me ghosteó.
example.en: We went out twice and then he stopped answering me.

words.note: "Mandarse una macana": to blunder. "Mandarse" also means to go boldly or do on impulse. Informal.

example.es: Me mandé una macana con el auto de mi viejo.
example.en: I made a mistake with my dad's car.

words.note: Lunfardo for eating, very common. In football, "morfarse la pelota" is to hog the ball.

example.es: Vamos a morfar algo, que me muero de hambre.
example.en: Let's eat something, I'm very hungry.

packs.name: Essentials VI
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Essentials VI
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: In Argentina "pararse" means to stand up, not just to stop. "Parate" is stand up.

example.es: Parate un segundo que te saco una foto.
example.en: Stand up for a second so I can take your picture.

words.note: To click with someone, often romantically: "pegamos onda enseguida". Informal.

example.es: Pegamos onda en la fiesta y ahora salimos.
example.en: We got along well at the party and now we're dating.

words.note: "Me pinta" is I feel like it; "¿pinta un asado?" is are we up for a barbecue?

example.es: ¿Pinta ir al cine esta noche?
example.en: Do you want to go to the movies tonight?

words.note: "¿Te prendés?" means are you in? To sign up for a plan or activity.

example.es: Vamos a jugar al fútbol, ¿te prendés?
example.en: We're going to play football, do you want to join?

words.note: "Rajar" is to fire or kick out: "lo rajaron". "Rajá de acá": get out of here. Informal.

example.es: Lo rajaron del laburo por llegar siempre tarde.
example.en: He got fired for always showing up late.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Everyday
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: The everyday Argentine word for scold, instead of regañar: "me retó la maestra".

example.es: Mi vieja me retó por llegar tarde.
example.en: My mom got angry at me for coming home late.

words.note: To scrape by or escape something: "zafé del examen". "Zafa": it's passable. Very common.

example.es: No estudié mucho, pero zafé con un cuatro.
example.en: I didn't study much, but I just passed with a four.

words.note: Informal: to cross a line, say or do something excessive. "¡Te zarpaste!" = you went too far.

example.es: Te zarpaste con el chiste sobre su mamá.
example.en: You went too far with the joke about his mom.

words.note: Besides hurry, in Argentina it means to corner or press someone for answers: "lo apuré y confesó".

example.es: Lo apuré un poco y terminó contando todo.
example.en: I pushed him a bit and he ended up telling everything.

words.note: To watch without getting involved, as if from a balcony.

example.es: Vos no ayudás, te quedás balconeando.
example.en: You don't help, you just watch.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Going deeper I
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: To tell on someone to a teacher, boss or the police.

example.es: Me botoneó con la profe.
example.en: He told the teacher on me.

words.note: To keep bothering or teasing someone. "Cargoso" is an annoying person.

example.es: Dejá de cargosear a tu hermano, que está estudiando.
example.en: Stop bothering your brother, he's studying.

words.note: To think up a plan or idea: "estoy craneando algo". Informal.

example.es: Estamos craneando una sorpresa para su cumple.
example.en: We're planning a surprise for her birthday.

words.note: To tear someone apart behind their back. Literally to skin an animal.

example.es: Se pasaron la cena cuereando a la ex de Martín.
example.en: They spent dinner saying bad things about Martín's ex.

words.note: "No curto el reggaetón": I'm not into reggaeton. Also to enjoy a place or a vibe: "curtir la playa".

example.es: Yo no curto mucho el reggaetón.
example.en: I don't really like reggaeton.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Going deeper II
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: Slang sense: to make fun of or show someone up: "me descansó". Youthful, informal.

example.es: Me descansaron todo el día por el corte de pelo.
example.en: They made fun of me all day because of my haircut.

words.note: To reveal a secret or rat someone out. "Deschavarse" is to give yourself away.

example.es: No me deschaves, que mi vieja no sabe nada.
example.en: Don't tell on me, my mom doesn't know anything.

words.note: To type up a recording, like an interview or class.

example.es: Me pasé la tarde desgrabando la entrevista.
example.en: I spent the afternoon transcribing the interview.

words.note: To hit the target or guess correctly: "la embocaste". Informal.

example.es: Con el regalo la embocaste, le encantó.
example.en: You got it right with the present, she loved it.

words.note: To eye someone up or keep an eye on them: "te está fichando". Informal.

example.es: Ese flaco te está fichando desde que llegamos.
example.en: That guy has been looking at you since we arrived.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Going deeper III
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: To go bankrupt or run out of money: "se fundió el negocio". Also to be worn out. Informal.

example.es: Se le fundió el negocio con la crisis.
example.en: His business failed because of the crisis.

words.note: To live off others or keep asking for things for free.

example.es: Siempre me garronea cigarrillos y nunca compra.
example.en: He always asks me for cigarettes and never buys any.

words.note: To be unfaithful: "lo gorrearon". From "poner los cuernos". Informal.

example.es: Se separaron porque ella lo gorreaba con un compañero.
example.en: They split up because she was cheating on him with a coworker.

words.note: To get something, good or bad: "ligar entradas", "ligar un reto". Not used for flirting.

example.es: Ligué dos entradas para el recital.
example.en: I got two tickets for the concert.

words.note: To say lies or nonsense. A "macana" is a bummer or a lie.

example.es: Dejá de macanear, eso nunca pasó.
example.en: Stop making things up, that never happened.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Going deeper IV
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: Asking someone for money, a smoke or a favor. Someone who does it a lot is a "manguero".

example.es: Me mangueó veinte lucas y nunca me las devolvió.
example.en: He asked me for twenty thousand pesos and never paid it back.

words.note: To grab or swipe with a quick hand movement, or snatch at something. Informal.

example.es: Me manoteó el celular de la mano en el bondi.
example.en: He grabbed the phone out of my hand on the bus.

words.note: To bring bad luck by saying something too early. Football fans are obsessed with it.

example.es: ¡No digas que ganamos, que lo mufás!
example.en: Don't say we won, you'll bring bad luck!

words.note: To burn through cash: "me patiné el sueldo". Informal.

example.es: Me patiné todo el aguinaldo en una semana.
example.en: I spent my whole bonus in a week.

words.note: To sneak a look: "pispeá qué hay en la heladera". Informal, playful.

example.es: Pispeé el regalo antes del cumple.
example.en: I looked at the present before the birthday.

packs.name: Going deeper V
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Going deeper V
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: Informal: to reveal someone's secret or call them out, often in public or online. "¡Me quemaste!" = you blew my cover.

example.es: No le cuentes a nadie, que me quemás con mi vieja.
example.en: Don't tell anyone, you'll get me in trouble with my mom.

words.note: Informal. Used by students for cutting class. "Hacerse la rata" means the same.

example.es: Me rateé del colegio para ir a la plaza con mis amigos.
example.en: I skipped school to go to the park with my friends.

words.note: Informal: to glance at or keep an eye on something, often sneakily. Also used for eyeing someone you like.

example.es: Relojeá si viene el colectivo mientras compro agua.
example.en: Watch for the bus while I buy water.

words.note: To calm down or get your act together: "rescatate". Youth slang, very common.

example.es: Rescatate un poco, ya te pasaste con el vino.
example.en: Calm down a bit, you've had too much wine.

words.note: To leave, often in a hurry: "me las tomo". "¡Tomátelas!": get lost. Informal.

example.es: Bueno, me las tomo que mañana madrugo.
example.en: Well, I'm leaving, I have to get up early tomorrow.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Everyday verbs · Rare gems
packs.about: The verbs Argentines use instead of the textbook ones.

words.note: From "covacha", a hovel. To hide something away in a safe spot. "Acovacharse": to hole up at home.

example.es: Acovachó la plata abajo del colchón.
example.en: He hid the money under the mattress.

words.note: From Italian "aggiornare". Used for modernizing things, laws or looks. Sometimes spelled "ayornar".

example.es: Hay que aggiornar la cocina, está igual que en los ochenta.
example.en: We need to update the kitchen, it's just like the eighties.

words.note: To lock a door with a key. Cerrar con llave is more common.

example.es: Acordate de llavear la puerta cuando salgas.
example.en: Remember to lock the door when you leave.

words.note: A "machete" is a cheat sheet. Copiarse is more common.

example.es: Lo agarraron macheteándose en el examen.
example.en: They caught him cheating on the exam.

words.note: Informal, mostly young people: to stay and hang out somewhere, often at someone's place or on a corner.

example.es: Nos quedamos ranchando en lo de Juan toda la tarde.
example.en: We stayed hanging out at Juan's place all afternoon.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Going out · Essentials I
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: Club where people dance cumbia and cuarteto; also the whole cumbia scene. Once looked down on, now mainstream.

example.es: El sábado nos vamos a una bailanta en Constitución.
example.en: On Saturday we're going to a cumbia club in Constitución.

words.note: Informal, from Italian. "Tomar unas birras": to have some beers.

example.es: ¿Vamos a tomar unas birras después del laburo?
example.en: Do you want to have some beers after work?

words.note: The word for a club or disco. "Ir al boliche" is the Saturday plan. Older sense: a small shop or bar.

example.es: El sábado vamos al boliche después de la previa.
example.en: On Saturday we're going to the club after drinking at home.

words.note: To kiss passionately. The go-to word among young people.

example.es: Anoche en el boliche chapó con tres chicos.
example.en: Last night at the club she kissed three guys.

words.note: A casual lover or friend with benefits, not a partner.

example.es: No es mi novio, es un chongo nomás.
example.en: He's not my boyfriend, just a casual partner.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Going out · Essentials II
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: To drink alcohol, usually a lot. Informal. "Vamos a chupar" means let's go drinking.

example.es: El sábado chupamos toda la noche en lo de Juan.
example.en: On Saturday we drank all night at Juan's.

words.note: To get very drunk. From "pedo", drunkenness.

example.es: Nos empedamos en el cumple de Nico.
example.en: We got very drunk at Nico's birthday party.

words.note: Slang for illegal drugs, especially cocaine. As an adjective it means cheap or fake.

example.es: Dicen que en esa fiesta había mucha falopa.
example.en: They say there were lots of drugs at that party.

words.note: Slang for a cigarette, and also a joint.

example.es: Salí al balcón a fumar un faso.
example.en: I went out on the balcony to smoke a cigarette.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Going out · Essentials III
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: "Ir de joda" is to go partying. "En joda" or "de joda" means just kidding.

example.es: ¿Vamos a la joda del sábado?
example.en: Are we going to the party on Saturday?

words.note: Casual meetup with friends, often with food and drinks.

example.es: El viernes hay juntada en casa, ¿venís?
example.en: There's a get-together at my place on Friday, are you coming?

words.note: To hook up with or pick someone up on a night out. "Levantó una mina" or "levantó un chabón".

example.es: Anoche en el boliche no levanté nada.
example.en: Last night at the club I didn't meet anyone.

words.note: The big muscly guy at the club door. Also any beefy gym guy.

example.es: El patovica no nos dejó entrar por las zapatillas.
example.en: The security guard didn't let us in because of our shoes.

words.note: A bottle of beer, usually a small one. "Unos porrones" is some beers.

example.es: Compramos unos porrones para ver el partido.
example.en: We bought some beers to watch the game.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Going out · Essentials IV
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: Drinks at someone's place before going out to the club. Can last hours.

example.es: Hacemos la previa en casa y después vamos al boliche.
example.en: We'll have drinks at my place and then go to the club.

words.note: Very common, informal. Also means a cigarette butt. "Sobre el pucho" means right away.

example.es: ¿Tenés un pucho? Me olvidé los míos en casa.
example.en: Do you have a cigarette? I left mine at home.

words.note: Argentines say "recital" for a live music show, especially rock or pop. "Ir a un recital".

example.es: Conseguí entradas para el recital del viernes en River.
example.en: I got tickets for Friday's concert at River.

words.note: To give someone signals that you're interested. "Me está tirando onda" means he's flirting with me.

example.es: Ese chico te está tirando onda hace una hora.
example.en: That guy has been flirting with you for an hour.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Going out · Everyday
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: Street slang for a small-time drug dealer. Also means a shady deal: "hicieron una transa".

example.es: Dicen que el de la esquina es transa.
example.en: They say the guy on the corner is a drug dealer.

words.note: The party that keeps going after the boliche closes, into the morning. Pronounced "áfter".

example.es: Salimos del boliche a las seis y nos fuimos a un after.
example.en: We left the club at six and went to another party.

words.note: Someone who loves going out to clubs. Also a nightclub owner.

example.es: Mi hermano es re bolichero, sale todos los fines de semana.
example.en: My brother really loves going out, he goes out every weekend.

words.note: Upbeat party music mixing cumbia, reggaeton and pop; also the party itself.

example.es: A esta hora el DJ pone puro cachengue.
example.en: At this hour the DJ plays nothing but party hits.

words.note: A glass or mug of draft beer. Pronounced "chop". "Un chopp y una picada".

example.es: Pedime un chopp bien frío, por favor.
example.en: Order me a really cold draft beer, please.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Going out · Going deeper I
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: Fast, cheerful dance music born in Córdoba, with La Mona Jiménez and Rodrigo as its legends.

example.es: En Córdoba los sábados se sale a bailar cuarteto.
example.en: In Córdoba on Saturdays people go out to dance cuarteto.

words.note: Cumbia from the working-class suburbs, with gritty lyrics. A fixture of any party.

example.es: En el cumple pusieron cumbia villera hasta las cinco.
example.en: At the birthday party they played street cumbia until five.

words.note: Slightly drunk and cheerful, before being really drunk.

example.es: Con dos fernets ya estaba medio entonado.
example.en: After two fernets I was already a little drunk.

words.note: From "escabio", booze. Slangy.

example.es: Volvió escabiado del cumpleaños y se durmió vestido.
example.en: He came back drunk from the party and slept in his clothes.

words.note: Slang for alcohol in general. "Traer el escabio" is to bring the drinks to a party.

example.es: ¿Quién trae el escabio para el cumple del sábado?
example.en: Who is bringing the drinks for Saturday's birthday party?

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Going out · Going deeper II
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: Playful name for fernet con Coca, the classic Argentine drink, especially in Córdoba.

example.es: Armate un fernando que ya llegan los chicos.
example.en: Make yourself a fernet and Coke, the guys are almost here.

words.note: A pass to get into a boliche without paying, usually from a promoter. "Tengo free hasta la una".

example.es: Tengo free para entrar antes de la una.
example.en: I can get in without paying before one.

words.note: A long night out going from place to place. "Irse de gira" is to go out and not come back till morning.

example.es: Anoche nos fuimos de gira y volví a las ocho.
example.en: Last night we went out partying and I got back at eight.

words.note: To play matchmaker: introduce two people hoping they hook up.

example.es: Le hice gancho a mi amiga con tu primo.
example.en: I introduced my friend to your cousin to see if they'd like each other.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Going out · Going deeper III
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: A big jug mixing whatever alcohol is around, shared at parties. Dangerous.

example.es: La jarra loca tenía de todo y me mató.
example.en: The jug of mixed drinks had everything in it and it made me very drunk.

words.note: An early-evening party at a boliche for under-18s, with no alcohol. Many teens' first night out.

example.es: A los catorce iba a la matinée todos los domingos.
example.en: At fourteen I went to the teen club every Sunday.

words.note: Street slang for cocaine, short for "mercadería" (merchandise).

example.es: En esa fiesta había merca por todos lados.
example.en: There was cocaine everywhere at that party.

words.note: Slang for a joint. Also means whistle, or penis in some contexts.

example.es: Se fumaron un pito en la terraza.
example.en: They smoked marijuana on the roof.

words.note: Jumping and shoving in the crowd at a rock show. "Meterse en el pogo".

example.es: Me metí en el pogo y perdí una zapatilla.
example.en: I went into the pushing crowd and lost a shoe.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: Going out · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: Short for "relaciones públicas", said "erre-erre-pe-pe": the person who sells tickets and puts you on the list.

example.es: Hablale al RRPP que nos pone en lista.
example.en: Talk to the promoter, he'll put us on the list.

words.note: Cheap wine in a Tetra Pak carton. Mocking but loved at student parties.

example.es: Compramos un tetra y un fernet para la previa.
example.en: We bought boxed wine and a fernet to drink before going out.

words.note: A late-night movie screening or TV slot, around midnight. Also staying up late in general.

example.es: Vamos a la función de trasnoche del sábado.
example.en: Let's go to the Saturday late-night showing.

words.note: Informal slang for a marijuana cigarette. "Porro" and "faso" are also common.

example.es: Estaban fumando un troncho en la plaza.
example.en: They were smoking marijuana in the park.

packs.name: Rare gems
packs.title: Going out · Rare gems
packs.about: Parties, bars, nights out and the morning after.

words.note: Lunfardo for drinking a lot, often to get drunk. Escabiarse means to get drunk.

example.es: Anoche escabiamos hasta las cuatro de la mañana.
example.en: Last night we were drinking until four in the morning.

words.note: Playful slang for a party with friends.

example.es: Mañana hay festichola en lo de Juli.
example.en: There's a party at Juli's place tomorrow.

words.note: Slang for cocaine, heard in rock and cumbia lyrics.

example.es: Dicen que el cantante estaba hasta las manos con la frula.
example.en: They say the singer used a lot of cocaine.

words.note: Old lunfardo, still heard with a wink: "agarrarse una mamúa" is to get plastered.

example.es: Anoche se agarró una mamúa bárbara en el casamiento.
example.en: Last night he got very drunk at the wedding.

words.note: Party slang: to crash after too much alcohol or drugs. "Estar quebrado" is to be wasted. "Quebrarse" can mean to break down crying.

example.es: Tomó tanto fernet que a las dos ya había quebrado.
example.en: He drank so much fernet he was very drunk by two.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Football · Essentials I
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: Cheer of support: "¡Aguante Boca!". As a noun it means endurance; "hacer el aguante" is to back someone.

example.es: ¡Aguante la Selección, carajo!
example.en: Let's go, national team, damn it!

words.note: Extra time in a match. Also used for an extension cord.

example.es: Ganamos en el alargue con un gol de cabeza.
example.en: We won in extra time with a goal with the head.

words.note: The goalie. Argentines say "arquero" rather than "portero"; the goal itself is "el arco".

example.es: El arquero atajó un penal en el último minuto.
example.en: The goalkeeper saved a penalty in the last minute.

words.note: A goalkeeper's stop. Goalkeepers "atajan"; the keeper is the "arquero".

example.es: ¡Qué atajada del Dibu en el último minuto!
example.en: What a save by Dibu in the last minute!

words.note: From "bosta", dung: rivals' nickname for Boca fans that the fans adopted proudly.

example.es: Mi viejo es bostero a muerte.
example.en: My dad is a die-hard Boca Juniors fan.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Football · Essentials II
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: A footballer's wife or girlfriend, often a celebrity. From "botines", football boots.

example.es: Salió en la tele con otra botinera famosa.
example.en: She was on TV with another famous footballer's girlfriend.

words.note: Studded football boots. "Botín" alone is one boot.

example.es: Me compré botines nuevos para el torneo.
example.en: I bought new football boots for the tournament.

words.note: The pitch or stadium. "Ir a la cancha" means going to watch your team live.

example.es: El domingo vamos a la cancha a ver a Racing.
example.en: On Sunday we're going to the stadium to see Racing.

words.note: In football, passing the ball between a rival's legs: "tirar un caño". Also means a pipe.

example.es: Le tiró un caño al defensor y la gente enloqueció.
example.en: He played the ball between the defender's legs and the crowd went crazy.

words.note: Short for "director técnico", said "de-te". Everyone has an opinion on the DT.

example.es: Si seguimos perdiendo, lo echan al DT.
example.en: If we keep losing, they'll fire the coach.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Football · Essentials III
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: The break in a football game. Also between seasons, "ropa de entretiempo".

example.es: En el entretiempo fuimos a comprar un choripán.
example.en: At half-time we went to buy a chorizo sandwich.

words.note: The stickers for World Cup albums. "Figurita repetida" is someone who's always around.

example.es: Me falta una sola figurita para llenar el álbum.
example.en: I'm just one sticker away from filling the album.

words.note: A casual game among friends, usually fútbol cinco. Also flashy play that gets nowhere.

example.es: Los jueves jugamos al fulbito con los del laburo.
example.en: On Thursdays we play casual soccer with the people from work.

words.note: Boca fans say it as a taunt, but River fans use it proudly too.

example.es: Mi viejo es gallina y yo soy de Boca.
example.en: My dad is a River fan and I support Boca.

words.note: A dribble past a rival, the art Maradona and Messi are famous for. The verb is "gambetear".

example.es: Messi hizo una gambeta y dejó a tres en el piso.
example.en: Messi pulled off a dribble and left three on the ground.

packs.name: Essentials IV
packs.title: Football · Essentials IV
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: Elsewhere often autogol. Also used for any self-inflicted mistake.

example.es: Perdimos por un gol en contra en el último minuto.
example.en: We lost because of an own goal in the last minute.

words.note: A football supporter. The hardcore organized fans are the "barra brava".

example.es: Soy hincha de Racing desde chiquito.
example.en: I've been a Racing fan since I was little.

words.note: A team's supporters as a group, singing in the stands. "La hinchada de Boca".

example.es: La hinchada no paró de cantar en todo el partido.
example.en: The fans didn't stop singing the whole match.

words.note: "¿Por quién hinchás?" asks your team. "No hinches" also means stop bugging me.

example.es: ¿Vos por quién hinchás?
example.en: Which team do you support?

words.note: To drop down a division. River's 2011 relegation is still the classic joke.

example.es: Si perdemos hoy, nos vamos a la B.
example.en: If we lose today, we drop to the second division.

packs.name: Essentials V
packs.title: Football · Essentials V
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: Nickname for Scaloni's Argentina side, 2022 World Cup champions.

example.es: La Scaloneta nos dio la tercera estrella.
example.en: Scaloni's team gave us the third star.

words.note: Table football, a classic in bars and clubs. From "mete gol", score a goal.

example.es: ¿Jugamos un metegol mientras esperamos la pizza?
example.en: Do you want to play table football while we wait for the pizza?

words.note: An informal, pick-up football match among friends or neighbors.

example.es: Armamos un picado en la plaza después del colegio.
example.en: We played a casual football game in the square after school.

words.note: The biggest derby in Argentina: Boca Juniors against River Plate. The whole country stops to watch.

example.es: El domingo hay superclásico y no se habla de otra cosa.
example.en: There's a Boca-River match on Sunday and nobody talks about anything else.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Football · Going deeper I
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: Named for the white and sky-blue shirt. Common in sports news; fans usually say "la Selección".

example.es: La albiceleste juega el martes en el Monumental.
example.en: The national team plays Tuesday at the Monumental.

words.note: A fake move, in football or in life. The verb is "amagar": to fake.

example.es: Con un amague lo dejó sentado al defensor.
example.en: With one fake move he left the defender on the ground.

words.note: The organized hardcore fan group of a club, often linked to violence and business. Also just "la barra".

example.es: La barra brava se quedó con las mejores entradas.
example.en: The violent fans kept the best tickets.

words.note: A fan chant sung in the stands, often mocking the rival.

example.es: La hinchada inventó un cantito nuevo para el clásico.
example.en: The fans made up a new song for the big match.

words.note: The classic number 10 who links midfield and attack. Riquelme is the textbook example.

example.es: A este equipo le falta un enganche como Riquelme.
example.en: This team needs a creative player like Riquelme.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Football · Going deeper II
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: The full calendar of matches in a tournament. From English, pronounced "fíxtur".

example.es: Mirá el fixture, nos toca River en la tercera fecha.
example.en: Look at the schedule, we play River in the third round.

words.note: Juggling the ball without letting it touch the ground. "Hacer jueguito".

example.es: El nene hace cien jueguitos sin que se le caiga.
example.en: The kid kicks the ball up a hundred times without dropping it.

words.note: The cheapest standing section of the stadium, where the loudest fans go.

example.es: Siempre voy a la popular con mi viejo.
example.en: I always go to the cheap standing area with my dad.

words.note: A River Plate fan or player, from the club's nickname "los Millonarios".

example.es: Mi viejo es millonario y mi vieja bostera.
example.en: My dad supports River and my mom supports Boca.

words.note: A player who never passes. From "morfar", to eat: he eats the ball.

example.es: Pasala, morfón, que estoy solo.
example.en: Pass it, you selfish player, I'm free.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Football · Going deeper III
packs.about: The words of the stands and the pitch.

words.note: Argentine spelling and pronunciation of "offside". "Estaba en orsai".

example.es: El gol no vale, estaba en orsai.
example.en: The goal doesn't count, he was offside.

words.note: Someone terrible at football, all kicks and no touch. Teasing among friends.

example.es: No me elijan, soy un patadura.
example.en: Don't pick me, I'm bad at football.

words.note: A player who doesn't show passion or fight for the shirt. A harsh fan insult.

example.es: Ese nueve es un pechofrío, no corre nunca.
example.en: That striker has no heart, he never runs.

words.note: The players of a team, used a lot in sports news.

example.es: El plantel entrenó a puertas cerradas.
example.en: The team trained behind closed doors.

words.note: Football: a very hard, powerful shot. Loved by commentators.

example.es: Le pegó de afuera del área, un taponazo al ángulo.
example.en: He hit it from outside the area, a very strong shot into the top corner.

packs.name: Essentials I
packs.title: Politics & society · Essentials I
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: A protest where people bang pots and pans from balconies or in the street.

example.es: Anoche hubo cacerolazo en todo el barrio.
example.en: Last night there was a pot-banging protest all over the neighborhood.

words.note: Made popular by Javier Milei to attack career politicians.

example.es: Dice que va a terminar con los privilegios de la casta.
example.en: He says he'll end the privileges of the political elite.

words.note: The ring of districts around the capital, where a third of the country lives. Key in every election.

example.es: Nací en el conurbano, en Lomas de Zamora.
example.en: I was born in the suburbs, in Lomas de Zamora.

words.note: The 2001 limit on withdrawing savings that set off a huge crisis.

example.es: Con el corralito mis viejos perdieron sus ahorros.
example.en: When the banks froze the money, my parents lost their savings.

words.note: A follower of ex-president Cristina Kirchner. Also an adjective.

example.es: Mi tío es re cristinista, no le hables de política.
example.en: My uncle is a big Cristina supporter, don't talk to him about politics.

packs.name: Essentials II
packs.title: Politics & society · Essentials II
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: Short for fascista. Used loosely for anyone authoritarian or hard right.

example.es: Mi tío es medio facho, no le hables de política.
example.en: My uncle is kind of a fascist, don't talk politics with him.

words.note: Political label for someone who hates Peronism, since the 1955 coup.

example.es: Mi abuelo era re gorila, odiaba a Perón.
example.en: My grandfather was a strong anti-Peronist, he hated Perón.

words.note: The deep split between Kirchnerists and anti-Kirchnerists that divides families and friends.

example.es: En mi familia la grieta arruina todos los asados.
example.en: In my family the political divide ruins every barbecue.

words.note: Political movement of Néstor and Cristina Kirchner, part of Peronism.

example.es: El kirchnerismo ganó en la provincia de Buenos Aires.
example.en: Kirchnerism won in Buenos Aires province.

packs.name: Essentials III
packs.title: Politics & society · Essentials III
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: Supporter of Néstor and Cristina Kirchner. Opponents say kuka.

example.es: Toda mi familia es kirchnerista.
example.en: My whole family is pro-Kirchner.

words.note: In Argentina it means pro free market and small state, not left-leaning like in the US.

example.es: Mi primo se hizo liberal y ahora habla solo de impuestos.
example.en: My cousin became a free-market supporter and now only talks about taxes.

words.note: A strike, from one sector to a "paro general". "Hay paro de colectivos": there are no buses today.

example.es: Mañana hay paro de trenes, así que voy en bondi.
example.en: Tomorrow there's a train strike, so I'm taking the bus.

words.note: The movement founded by Juan Perón; still the central divide of Argentine politics.

example.es: En mi familia el peronismo es casi una religión.
example.en: In my family, Peronism is almost a religion.

words.note: A supporter of Perón's movement. Also an adjective: "un gobierno peronista".

example.es: Mi abuelo era peronista de toda la vida.
example.en: My grandpa was a lifelong Peronist.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Politics & society · Everyday
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: A protester who blocks roads, a symbol of Argentine social movements since the 90s.

example.es: Los piqueteros cortaron la avenida toda la mañana.
example.en: The protesters blocked the avenue all morning.

words.note: Literally left-handed. Politically, a leftist; used a lot as a jab in political arguments.

example.es: Mi tío dice que todos los profesores son zurdos.
example.en: My uncle says all teachers are leftists.

words.note: The French word used for a presidential second round. Pronounced "ba-lo-TASH".

example.es: Si nadie gana en primera vuelta, hay ballottage.
example.en: If nobody wins the first round, there's a second round.

words.note: Short for "bolchevique". Teasing or dismissive label for a leftist.

example.es: Mi tío dice que todos los profesores son bolches.
example.en: My uncle says all the teachers are communists.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper I
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: A presidential speech that all TV and radio stations must air at once.

example.es: Cortaron la novela por una cadena nacional.
example.en: They cut the soap opera for a presidential broadcast.

words.note: To stall a project by leaving it in a drawer. Common about bills in Congress.

example.es: El Congreso cajoneó el proyecto de ley.
example.en: Congress put the new law on hold.

words.note: Member of La Cámpora, the Kirchnerist youth group named after President Héctor Cámpora.

example.es: Mi primo es camporista y milita en el barrio.
example.en: My cousin is in La Cámpora and is a political activist in the neighborhood.

words.note: Government limits on buying dollars, which feed the blue market. "Salir del cepo" means lifting them.

example.es: Con el cepo no se podían comprar más de doscientos dólares.
example.en: With the controls, you couldn't buy more than two hundred dollars.

words.note: The old compulsory service, ended in 1994. Folk origin: "corre, limpia, barre".

example.es: Mi viejo hizo la colimba en el sur.
example.en: My dad did his military service down south.

packs.name: Going deeper II
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper II
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: Protesters blocking a road or highway, the signature tactic of piqueteros.

example.es: Hay un corte de ruta en la Panamericana, andá por otro lado.
example.en: There's a road block on the highway, go another way.

words.note: To publicly expose someone, online or with a protest outside their home. Also "escracharse": to crash hard.

example.es: Lo escracharon en las redes por lo que dijo.
example.en: He was publicly shamed on social media for what he said.

words.note: The usual word for a trade union. "Los gremios" have huge political weight in Argentina.

example.es: El gremio de los docentes convocó a un paro.
example.en: The teachers' union called a strike.

words.note: The official name of the Peronist party is Partido Justicialista, or PJ.

example.es: Es el candidato del partido justicialista.
example.en: He's the candidate of the Peronist party.

packs.name: Going deeper III
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper III
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: Short for "Casa Rosada", the pink government house in Plaza de Mayo.

example.es: Hay una marcha frente a la Rosada.
example.en: There's a march in front of the presidential palace.

words.note: The 1990s era and politics of president Carlos Menem: privatizations, the peso-dollar peg, flashy excess.

example.es: En el menemismo todos viajaban a Miami con el uno a uno.
example.en: Under Menem everyone flew to Miami, with one peso equal to one dollar.

words.note: The libertarian movement around president Javier Milei, known for "la motosierra" spending cuts.

example.es: El mileísmo ganó fuerza entre los pibes más jóvenes.
example.en: Mileism gained strength among young people.

words.note: Member of Montoneros, the armed Peronist left of the 1970s. Still a charged political word.

example.es: Su tío fue montonero en los años setenta.
example.en: His uncle was a guerrilla in the seventies.

words.note: Someone on the public payroll who only shows up to collect, like eating gnocchi on the 29th.

example.es: Ese es un ñoqui, aparece solo para cobrar.
example.en: That guy's a fake employee, he only shows up to get paid.

packs.name: Going deeper IV
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper IV
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: The mandatory open primary elections, said as one word: "las PASO".

example.es: En las PASO ganó un candidato que nadie esperaba.
example.en: An unexpected candidate won the primary elections.

words.note: A politician whose image scares off voters for their own party.

example.es: Ese candidato es un piantavotos, nadie lo banca.
example.en: That candidate loses votes, nobody can stand him.

words.note: Derogatory for someone living on a "plan social", welfare benefits. Politically loaded.

example.es: Mi tío dice planero a cualquiera que no le cae bien.
example.en: My uncle says anyone he doesn't like lives off welfare.

words.note: A neighborhood political operator who hands out favors and mobilizes voters for a party.

example.es: El puntero del barrio organizó los micros para el acto.
example.en: The local party boss organized the buses for the political event.

packs.name: Going deeper V
packs.title: Politics & society · Going deeper V
packs.about: Parties, protests and the country in the news.

words.note: Political wheeling and dealing, deals made behind closed doors. "Rosquear" is the verb; a "rosquero" lives for it.

example.es: Esa ley salió por pura rosca entre los bloques.
example.en: That law passed through secret deals between the parties.

words.note: A sudden steep rise in gas, power or transport rates. Always a political fight.

example.es: Con el tarifazo, la boleta de luz vino el triple.
example.en: With the big price rise, the electricity bill was three times higher.

words.note: Almost always plural, "las tratativas". Common in the news for business or political talks.

example.es: Las tratativas con el sindicato siguen sin acuerdo.
example.en: Negotiations with the union still have no deal.

words.note: Follower of Raúl Alfonsín, first president after the 1983 return to democracy. Used in politics talk.

example.es: Mi viejo es radical, alfonsinista de toda la vida.
example.en: My dad is a Radical, a lifelong Alfonsín supporter.

words.note: Mocking term for someone who goes to political rallies for a free choripán. Derogatory.

example.es: Dicen que son choripaneros, pero van por convicción.
example.en: They say they go for the free food, but they go because they believe in it.

packs.name: Essentials
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Essentials
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: The everyday name for fireflies, seen on summer nights.

example.es: En el campo de mi abuela hay bichitos de luz.
example.en: At my grandma's farm there are fireflies.

words.note: The little bug that rolls into a ball. Every Argentine kid has played with one.

example.es: Los chicos juntaron bichos bolita en el jardín.
example.en: The kids collected small round bugs in the garden.

words.note: A farm smaller than an "estancia", often near town. From Quechua.

example.es: Los fines de semana vamos a la chacra de mis tíos.
example.en: On weekends we go to my aunt and uncle's farm.

words.note: A big cattle ranch in the pampas. Many now host tourists for asados and horse rides.

example.es: Hicimos un día de campo en una estancia.
example.en: We spent a country day at a ranch.

words.note: The horseman of the pampas. As an adjective it means helpful: "una gauchada" is a favor.

example.es: Mi abuelo era gaucho y domaba caballos.
example.en: My grandfather was a cowboy and tamed horses.

packs.name: Everyday
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Everyday
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: Any weed or wild herb. Herbs added to mate are also "yuyos".

example.es: El jardín está lleno de yuyos, hay que cortar el pasto.
example.en: The garden is full of weeds, we need to cut the grass.

words.note: Loose pleated pants worn by gauchos and country folk. Not to be confused with panties.

example.es: Para la jineteada se puso bombacha de campo y alpargatas.
example.en: For the rodeo he wore gaucho trousers and canvas shoes.

words.note: Accordion-based folk music and dance from northeastern Argentina.

example.es: En Corrientes todos los fines de semana hay bailes de chamamé.
example.en: In Corrientes there are chamamé dances every weekend.

words.note: A classic game at school fairs and rural festivals.

example.es: En la fiesta del pueblo ganamos la cinchada.
example.en: We won the tug of war at the town festival.

words.note: The long knife gauchos carry at the back of the belt, for eating and fighting.

example.es: El gaucho sacó el facón para cortar el asado.
example.en: The gaucho took out his knife to cut the asado.

packs.name: Going deeper I
packs.title: Countryside & gauchos · Going deeper I
packs.about: The pampa, the gaucho and life outside the city.

words.note: Gaucho bronco-riding contest, big at country festivals like Jesús María.

example.es: Fuimos a ver la jineteada en el festival de Jesús María.
example.en: We went to watch the rodeo at the Jesús María festival.

words.note: Guaraní name everyone uses in the north and many use in Buenos Aires.

example.es: Había un mamboretá verde en la ventana.
example.en: There was a green praying mantis on the window.

words.note: A man from the countryside, the modern gaucho. Also "fellow countryman".

example.es: Un paisano nos indicó el camino al pueblo.
example.en: A countryman showed us the way to town.

words.note: A hired worker on a farm or ranch. "Peón de campo" is the full phrase.

example.es: El peón se levanta a las cinco para ordeñar.
example.en: The farm worker gets up at five to milk the cows.

words.note: The old rural store and bar where gauchos met to drink, play cards and sing.

example.es: Paramos en una pulpería vieja a tomar algo.
example.en: We stopped at an old country store for a drink.
